issues.author: WhenWen
issues.body:
Benchmark results for the RMNP optimizer added in #8950, run at the completed 130M
settings from #6301 so the numbers are directly comparable to that submission.

## Summary

RMNP trails a freshly-tuned Muon baseline by **0.032 C4 BPB** at 130M. A 32x
learning-rate sweep places RMNP's optimum at **0.003**, the default already used in
#8950, so the gap is not a matter of LR tuning. Throughput is unaffected: MFU is
flat across the sweep and equal to Muon's.

## Results

All runs: Qwen3 130M, FineWeb-Edu 10B, seq 4096, batch 128, 4959 steps
(2.60B tokens), seed 0, v5p-8 in us-central1. Only the matrix LR varies.

| Run | Matrix LR | C4 BPB | vs Muon | MFU |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Muon (fresh baseline) | 0.016 | **1.16754** | — | 23.789% |
| #6301 reference | — | 1.16656 | −0.001 | 23.111% |
| RMNP | **0.003** | **1.19958** | **+0.032** | 23.787% |
| RMNP | 0.006 | 1.20263 | +0.035 | 23.575% |
| RMNP | 0.012 | 1.21668 | +0.049 | 23.764% |
| RMNP | 0.024 | 1.22354 | +0.056 | 23.778% |
| RMNP | 0.0015 | 1.22716 | +0.060 | 23.859% |
| RMNP | 0.00075 | 1.27212 | +0.105 | 23.849% |

## Observations

**The LR curve is single-minimum over a 32x range**, with the minimum at the
default 0.003. Tuning does not move the optimum.

**The gap is not LR mis-tuning.** The two best LRs differ by 0.00305 BPB, while the
distance to Muon is 0.03204 — roughly 10x larger.

**No throughput tradeoff.** MFU spans 23.58–23.86% across the sweep and matches
Muon's 23.789%, so the quality gap is not being paid for with speed.

**The baseline is trustworthy.** The fresh Muon run reproduces the #6301 reference
to within 0.001 BPB. This control mattered: both fresh runs reach ~639k tok/s versus
the reference's ~621k, so comparing RMNP's MFU against the archived number alone
would have shown a spurious ~3% speedup attributable to library changes rather than
to the optimizer.

## Caveats

- **One seed per point.** The 0.032 gap to Muon is far outside plausible seed noise,
  but the within-RMNP ordering (e.g. 0.003 vs 0.006, which differ by 0.003 BPB) is
  not resolved by this data.
- **130M only.** #6301 also reports completed 300M and 520M comparisons; whether the
  gap narrows with scale is untested here.
- Four runs took preemptions on preemptible capacity (lr012 three times, lr0015 /
  lr006 / lr024 once each). All resumed from checkpoint with `failures=0` and
  completed the full 4959 steps, so final metrics are unaffected.

## Reproduction

Optimizer implementations taken unchanged from #8950 at `d013891f9`. Each run:

```
python -m experiments.rmnp_speedrun \
  --optimizer {rmnp|muon} --learning-rate <lr> --run-id <id> --run
```

Shared recipe: linear schedule, no warmup, last 80% decay to zero; momentum 0.95
with Nesterov; Adam beta1 0.8 / beta2 0.98, eps 1e-15, Adam LR 0.0032; weight decay
0.1; global grad clip 1.0; bf16 compute with fp32 master params. Muon additionally
uses `muon_epsilon=1e-5`. Evaluation is the full C4 validation cache every 1000
steps and at the end.

W&B runs are in `marin-community/speedrun` under the group
`rmnp-pr8950-qwen3-130m-20260920`.

## Suggested next steps

1. Seed-variance runs at 0.003 and 0.006 to firm up the within-RMNP ordering.
2. Repeat at the 300M / 520M rungs to test whether the gap is scale-dependent.

issues.author: claude[bot]
issues.body:
## Problem

Endpoint lease renewal currently reuses the full `RegisterEndpoint` RPC, one call per endpoint per renewal interval (`EndpointLeaseRenewer.tick` → `_renew_one` → `self._register(lease.request)` in [`endpoint_client.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/client/endpoint_client.py#L274-L296)). Reusing register made the switchover trivial — existing clients always call `register`, so register-or-renew needed no new client surface — but it means each renewal re-sends the entire registration payload and does a full register's worth of work server-side.

With many endpoints per task this is more expensive than it needs to be (full re-registration cost × N endpoints × renewal frequency) and increases staleness pressure, since a cheaper renew could run more frequently. Raised by @ravwojdyla in PR #6728 review.

## Proposal

Split renewal from registration: add a cheap, batchable renew path that only carries the `endpoint_id`s (and requested lease duration), so one RPC can renew all of a client's leases at once. The renewer already iterates due leases in `tick`; it could collect them and issue a single batch-renew instead of N register calls.

Sketch:
- New `RenewEndpointLease(s)` RPC taking a list of `endpoint_id`s + a lease duration, returning the granted deadlines (and which ids were not found / expired).
- `EndpointLeaseRenewer.tick` batches all due leases into one call; `_renew_one` per-endpoint retry/backoff bookkeeping folds into a per-batch (or per-id-within-batch) result.
- Keep register-grants-a-lease as-is for the initial registration.

## Notes / priority

Low priority in practice: we typically have ~1 endpoint per task, so the per-renewal cost is small today. Tracking it so it isn't lost once endpoint-per-task counts grow.

Part of #6722. Follow-up from PR #6728.

issues.author: rjpower
issues.body:
## Summary

HF-format checkpoint export should be a separate `export_hf` `ArtifactStep` that depends on a `LevanterCheckpoint`, instead of an inline callback inside the training run. The inline export is forced on for every run and **cannot succeed on a multi-host TPU**, so multi-host training jobs crash at end-of-training even though training, eval, and the native checkpoint all succeeded.

## How it surfaced

End-to-end validation of the lazy `ArtifactStep` model on `v5litepod-16` (a 4-host v5e gang) ran the full graph correctly — tokenize → Levanter cache → train. Training completed all steps, the held-out eval ran (`eval loss: 9.805`), and the native tensorstore checkpoint was written. The job then failed in the inline HF export:

```
File "lib/levanter/src/levanter/compat/hf_checkpoints.py", line 1135, in save_pretrained
    shard_numpy = {k: np.asarray(v) for k, v in shard_weights.items()}
File ".../jax/_src/array.py", line 625, in _value
RuntimeError: Fetching value for `jax.Array` that spans non-addressable
(non process local) devices is not possible. You can use
`jax.experimental.multihost_utils.process_allgather` ...
```

One host exited 1; the gang `cosched_failed`; the step wrote no `artifact.json`.

## Root cause

- **Inline HF export runs on the training mesh.** `save_pretrained` materializes each tensor with `np.asarray(global_array)` (`hf_checkpoints.py:1135`). The `reshard(PartitionSpec())` at `:430` replicates a leaf but the replicated **global** array still spans non-addressable devices across hosts, so it is not `is_fully_addressable` and `np.asarray` raises. `max_shard_size` only shards the **output files**, not the device gather. There is no `process_allgather` / `addressable_shards` / `is_fully_addressable` path anywhere in the HF save path — it is an **unconditional multi-host failure**.
- **The native (tensorstore) checkpoint is multi-host-safe** — each process writes its own addressable shards via JAX's GSPMD array serialization — which is why resumption checkpoints survive but the HF export does not.
- **It is forced on with no opt-out.** `bake_output_path` unconditionally sets `hf_save_path = <output_path>/hf` (`training.py:199`), and the trainer runs all hooks with `force=True` at end-of-training (`trainer.py:560,573`), so every run gets a forced final `save_pretrained` regardless of `hf_save_steps`. The `train_lm` API exposes no way to disable it.

## Proposed solution: a separate `export_hf` ArtifactStep

The building blocks already exist and are currently **unwired** (referenced by zero experiments/steps):

- `lib/marin/src/marin/export/levanter_checkpoint.py::convert_checkpoint_to_hf` submits a **separate Fray job** running `levanter.main.export_lm_to_hf`, defaulting to **single-host CPU**, loading the saved **tensorstore** checkpoint into its own mesh and resharding — where every array is fully addressable, so `np.asarray` works.
- `LevanterCheckpoint` (`training.py:56-86`) already exposes `.checkpoint_dir` (the tensorstore root) and `.load`. A downstream `export_hf(checkpoint_handle)` step would declare the train handle as a `dep`, pull `LevanterCheckpoint(path=ctx.artifact_path(train)).checkpoint_dir`, and run `convert_checkpoint_to_hf` on its own right-sized resources. The conversion needs no training devices.

This decouples export from training (training can never again be failed by export), makes the HF artifact independently cacheable and re-runnable, and side-steps the multi-host crash for the common case.

## Two layers of work

1. **Decouple (fixes the crash + the architecture).** Stop forcing inline `hf_save_path` in `bake_output_path`; provide an `export_hf` ArtifactStep wrapping `convert_checkpoint_to_hf`. Small/medium models export on single-host CPU with no levanter change. Migrate experiments that consume `<output_path>/hf` to the step.
2. **"Builtin" multi-host-safe export (for models too large for one host).** A single host cannot hold a giant model, so the export step itself would need a real gather — `process_allgather` / per-host sharded safetensors — which levanter's HF writer lacks today. This is a levanter fix, needed regardless of inline-vs-step.

## Blast radius

Forced inline `<output_path>/hf` is currently produced by **every** training run, so other experiments likely consume it. Removing it from `bake_output_path` is a migration (each consumer adds the `export_hf` step).

## Key references

- `lib/marin/src/marin/training/training.py:188-200` — `bake_output_path` forces `hf_save_path`
- `lib/levanter/src/levanter/compat/hf_checkpoints.py:1135` (`save_pretrained`), `:430` (insufficient reshard), `:1305` (callback)
- `lib/levanter/src/levanter/trainer.py:560,573` — forced `run_hooks(force=True)` final save
- `lib/marin/src/marin/export/levanter_checkpoint.py` — `convert_checkpoint_to_hf` (unwired building block)
- `lib/levanter/src/levanter/main/export_lm_to_hf.py` — single-host CPU conversion entry
- `lib/marin/src/marin/training/training.py:56-86` — `LevanterCheckpoint` (`.checkpoint_dir`, `.load`)

_Filed from an end-to-end validation session for the lazy ArtifactStep / executor-context adoption work._

**Relevant code**
- [`training.py:119-143`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/training/training.py#L119-L143) — `bake_output_path` forces `hf_save_path`
- [`hf_checkpoints.py:1135`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/compat/hf_checkpoints.py#L1135) — `np.asarray` on global array; [`:430`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/compat/hf_checkpoints.py#L430) — insufficient reshard
- [`trainer.py:560-573`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/trainer.py#L560-L573) — forced final `run_hooks(force=True)`
- [`export/levanter_checkpoint.py:123-193`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/export/levanter_checkpoint.py#L123-L193) — `convert_checkpoint_to_hf_step` (exists, unwired)
- [`evaluation/run.py:139-140`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/run.py#L139-L140) — consumer strips `/hf`

# Proposed approach (for review — not a PR)

Three separable changes; (1) is the actual crash fix and is small, (2)+(3) are the larger migration/levanter work.

1. **Stop forcing inline export.** Drop the `hf_save_path` assignment from `bake_output_path` (and its docstring/`DEFAULT_HF_CHECKPOINTS_PATH` use). This alone unblocks multi-host training — the final forced `save_pretrained` no longer runs. Self-contained, but it removes an artifact every run currently produces, so it can't merge without (2).
2. **Wire `convert_checkpoint_to_hf_step` as the replacement.** The ExecutorStep already exists; add it downstream of training for each consumer of `<output_path>/hf` (depends on the train handle's `checkpoints/` dir, runs on single-host CPU). Migrate the ~4 experiments + eval to consume the step's output instead of `<output_path>/hf`.
3. **(Separate, levanter) multi-host-safe builtin export** for models too big for one host: add `process_allgather`/per-host sharded-safetensors to `save_pretrained`. Needed regardless of inline-vs-step; out of scope for the decouple.

Open questions for a human before implementation:
- Land on top of the executor-context/ArtifactStep branch, or as an independent `ExecutorStep`-based change on `main`? The issue frames it as `ArtifactStep`, which doesn't exist on `main` yet.
- Keep `bake_output_path` setting `hf_save_path` behind an explicit opt-in flag (for single-host runs that want inline export), or remove it entirely and always use the step?

issues.body:
🤖 Follow-up to the lazy-artifact migration (PR #6649).

## Context

The canary ferry (`experiments/ferries/canary_ferry.py`) and `save_logprobs`
(`lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/save_logprobs.py`) both need to **force packing on
every component** of an `LmDataConfig` — the canary because the `gpu_fa4_thd` attention
kernel only handles full causal windows, `save_logprobs` because it always packs.

PR #6649 deduplicated the two copies into one helper,
`marin.processing.tokenize.data_configs.with_pack(data, pack)`, which rewrites every
cache-backed component via `dataclasses.replace`. That removes the duplication but is
still a **post-hoc rewrite** of an already-assembled mixture.

## Why this is still a workaround

Packing is a load-time view, not a cache property: `dataset_for_component`
(`lib/levanter/src/levanter/data/text/datasets.py`) wraps the *same* `TreeCache` in a
`PackedTokenDataset` when `pack` is set, else a plain `CausalLmDataset`. So toggling
`pack` never re-tokenizes anything. Packing is applied **per component, before**
`MixtureDataset` combines them by weight — which is correct (packing the mixed stream
would glue documents from different sources into one example and break per-source
weighting/segmentation), so it can't move "to the top" of the dataset graph.

The real gap is config ergonomics. `LmDataConfig.block_cross_document_attention` is a
**top-level field** that fans out to every component at construction. `pack` is the only
one of these cross-cutting knobs with no top-level override — so "pack the whole mixture"
can only be expressed by reaching into `.components` and rewriting each leaf.

## Proposed cleanup

Add a top-level `pack: bool | int | Literal["pad"] | None = None` to `LmDataConfig`
(levanter), symmetric with `block_cross_document_attention`, and apply it as an override
in `dataset_for_component`:

```python
pack = config.pack if config.pack is not None else _effective_pack(component)
```

`None` preserves today's per-component behavior; set it and the whole mixture packs.
Then:

- thread `pack` through `marin.experiment.data.mixture(...)` so the canary becomes
  `mixture(ctx, {slimpajama: 1.0}, pack=1 if thd else None)`;
- `save_logprobs._force_pack_data` collapses to
  `replace(data, pack=True, block_cross_document_attention=True)`;
- delete `with_pack` and its two call sites.

This is a levanter change (one field + one override line + tests), which is why it was
deferred out of the migration PR. Tag with `agent-generated`.

issues.body:
## Description
Verify CE path behavior on a fresh readable May profile so we can isolate whether CE contributes to remaining forward/backward bottlenecks.

Parent tracker: #6693

### Definition of Done
- A readable profile for May shape is generated (or existing run is reused).
- B-tiled attribution rows are identified and stable.
- Notes are added on the dominant CE kernels and any practical optimization levers.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Actionability check — clear DoD, but this is a profiling/investigation task (no code defect)
- [x] Locate CE B-tiled path + profiling attribution tooling
- [x] Duplicate-work preflight (#5510 is the prior CE investigation)
- [x] Post research + reproducible approach (no PR — needs profiler runs + W&B artifacts I can't access)

# Research

This is a profiling investigation, not a code fix: the DoD is "generate/reuse a readable May profile, identify B-tiled attribution rows, note dominant CE kernels + levers." It needs a live May profile artifact (W&B) and the profiler stack — out of scope for a PR. Below is everything needed to execute it.

The **B-tiled CE path** is the full-vocab batched-XLA forward/backward used on H100. Attribution rows surface through `marin.profiling`, which buckets every CE kernel into the `loss_xent` semantic family via regex on `linear_softmax_cross_entropy_loss|softmax_cross_entropy|xent`.

**Relevant code**
- [`batched_xla.py#L317`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/kernels/pallas/fused_cross_entropy_loss/batched_xla.py#L317) — `_linear_softmax_cross_entropy_loss_full_vocab_b_tiled` (B-tiled forward)
- [`batched_xla.py#L552`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/kernels/pallas/fused_cross_entropy_loss/batched_xla.py#L552) — `_backward_b_tiled_from_lse` (B-tiled backward)
- [`batched_xla.py#L369`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/kernels/pallas/fused_cross_entropy_loss/batched_xla.py#L369) — `_h100_full_vocab_b_tiled_block_size` (selects B-block, e.g. 8192)
- [`semantics.py#L13`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/profiling/semantics.py#L13) — `loss_xent` family regex (the CE attribution bucket)
- [`query.py#L268`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/profiling/query.py#L268) — `_semantic_families_for_summary` (CE exclusive-time rows)

# Proposed approach (for the owner — needs infra)

1. **Get a readable May profile.** Reuse the May215 run referenced in #6693, or take a fresh non-truncated trace. Prior CE work (#5510) repeatedly hit empty `step_time` and trace truncation at 1,000,000 events — verify the reused trace is complete before trusting attribution.

2. **Summarize → CE rows** with the existing CLI (pulls the profiler dir from W&B and aggregates the `loss_xent` family):
   ```bash
   python -m marin.profiling.cli summarize \
     --run-target <may-run-id> --entity marin-community --project marin \
     --breakdown-mode exclusive_per_track --output /tmp/may.json
   python -m marin.profiling.cli query --summary /tmp/may.json \
     --question "loss_xent"   # CE family exclusive time + hot ops
   ```
   The B-tiled rows show up as `linear_softmax_cross_entropy_loss` ops; confirm the selected B-block matches `_h100_full_vocab_b_tiled_block_size` and that rows are stable across steps (drop warmup via `--warmup-steps`).

3. **Notes / levers.** Capture CE % of step time and the dominant kernels. Known levers from #5510: XLA streaming is the agreed default (dlwh: "just make xla streaming the default everywhere… for big models it won't be much of a bottleneck"); the H100 native Pallas CE forward does not lower (fp32 LM-head weight tile exceeds the shared-mem guard), and the hybrid XLA-fwd + custom-streaming-bwd gave ~15% CE-only / ~11% tok/s in microbench but no proven end-to-end step-time win.

**Recommendation:** if the May profile shows CE is a small fraction of fwd/bwd time, record that and close the row in #6693 with XLA streaming as the documented default — no native-CE rewrite. Reserve a narrower H100 kernel task only if CE is a measurable bottleneck.

No PR opened — this is investigation work requiring profiler runs and W&B artifacts. Happy to turn any concrete finding into a doc/code change once a profile is available.

Config diff between the two is exactly one substantive key (`cross_entropy_implementation`), so it's a clean A/B.

## B-tiled path identified (DoD ✓)
- "B-tiled" = `_linear_softmax_cross_entropy_loss_full_vocab_b_tiled` ([`batched_xla.py#L317`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/kernels/pallas/fused_cross_entropy_loss/batched_xla.py#L317)), gated by `_h100_full_vocab_b_tiled_block_size` (H100 + bf16 + `B≥8192` + `V≥65536` → block **8192**; constants `_H100_FULL_VOCAB_B_TILED_BLOCK_SIZE=8192`, `_H100_FULL_VOCAB_B_TILED_MIN_BATCH=8192`, `_LARGE_VOCAB_THRESHOLD=65536`).
- Impl→run mapping ([`api.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/kernels/pallas/fused_cross_entropy_loss/api.py)): `'xla'`→`linear_softmax_cross_entropy_loss_xla` (streaming); `'pallas_gpu'`→**renamed to `'batched_xla'`**→`_linear_softmax_cross_entropy_loss_batched_xla_impl`→on H100 dispatches to `_full_vocab_b_tiled` @ 8192.
- This run qualifies (vocab 128256 ≥ 65536, B≥8192), so **the B-tiled rows live in `MAY-217-PALLASCEV8192`** — the `V8192` in the name is the 8192 B-tile / custom-bwd V-block. Stable across the profiled steps; no trace truncation (247k / 356k events, `suspected_truncation=False`).

## A/B result — B-tiled is the win, not a remaining bottleneck (DoD ✓)
Throughput (W&B summary; **identical loss 11.7933 ⇒ numerically equivalent**):

| metric | XLA streaming | B-tiled @8192 | Δ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| final MFU | 16.34 | 19.12 | **+17.0%** |
| mean MFU | 13.59 | 15.87 | +16.8% |
| tokens/s | 75,570 | 88,430 | +17.0% |
| step time | 0.4336 s | 0.3706 s | −14.5% |

Profile attribution (exclusive device time over the capture window):

| | XLA streaming | B-tiled @8192 | Δ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| device compute | 6107 ms | 5111 ms | −996 ms |
| CE fusions (bucketed in `other`) | 3986 ms / n=35,248 | 3456 ms / n=14,928 | −530 ms / **−20,320 kernels** |

Consistent with the historical A/B in #4312 (CE `1.397s → 0.380s`, −72.8% CE kernel time).

## Dominant CE kernels
CE lowers to many small **unnamed fusion / `_lambda_` kernels** — the LM-head matmul (`[8192×2560×128256]` tiles) plus softmax/logsumexp reductions — bucketed into the `other` family. The streaming path spins **~20k more** of these kernels than b-tiled for identical work; that kernel-count blowup *is* the CE cost, and b-tiled@8192 collapses it.

## Levers / recommendation
- Keep **`batched_xla` (b-tiled @8192)** as the H100 CE default — it's already what the `May402+` baselines run (`PALLASCE`), +17% MFU, numerically identical. For this d2560/B8/vocab-128k shape CE is non-trivial, so "just use XLA streaming everywhere for big models" does **not** apply here.
- After b-tiled, CE is no longer the leading fwd/bwd cost — collectives (ring gather/scatter ~16%) and MoE expert/transport dominate (see #4312). **Recommend closing the CE row** once the reproduction below confirms.

## Tooling gaps found (filing separately)
1. `marin.profiling.cli summarize --run-target <grug run>` fails — grug `marin_moe` runs nest config at `trainer.trainer.log_dir` (resolver expects `trainer.log_dir`) and `log_dir='logs'` is ephemeral on the CW pod. Workaround that works: `summarize --artifact <run>-profiler:v0`.
2. `marin.profiling.semantics` `loss_xent` regex doesn't match GPU CE kernels (unnamed fusions) → CE is invisible as a family on GPU xplane. Needs `jax.named_scope` around the CE/LM-head or shape-based attribution.

## Next: reproduce the A/B
The above reuses existing artifacts; **we will reproduce the pair fresh** to confirm the delta on current `main`, flipping only `model.cross_entropy_implementation` between `batched_xla` (b-tiled@8192) and `xla`. Each run is a single 8×H100 CoreWeave node, ~15 min end-to-end (the science is ~5 s of steps; the rest is node bring-up + compile + 2-step profiler capture). Will post the reproduced numbers here.

🤖 Update: reproduced the runs — on current `main`, B-tiled fused CE is silently bypassed in sharded training and is the *slowest* CE arm; one-line policy fix restores it

Correcting my [earlier comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6695) (posted before reproducing) on two points: (1) the CE **per-device batch is 4096**, not `B ≥ 8192` (the +17% A/B there was a June run on the earlier `pallas_gpu` impl); (2) on current `main`, `batched_xla` is **not** the default win — at per-device 4096 it bypasses B-tiled and is slower than `xla`. This fix restores the win.

- **Root cause:** `batched_xla`'s full-vocab B-tiled path only activates at per-call `B ≥ 8192` (the `_H100_FULL_VOCAB_B_TILED_MIN_BATCH` gate, introduced with the current `batched_xla` path in #6572). Training shards the CE 8-way (`loss.py` `shard_map`), so each device sees `32768 / 8 = 4096 < 8192` → fast path bypassed → ~2× slower FA-style streaming fallback.
- **Why the fallback is slow (profile-verified):** it fragments the `[B,H]@[H,V]` LM-head matmul into an unrolled vocab-tile loop — `num_v_blocks = ⌈128256/1024⌉ = 126` small width-`1024` GEMMs (+ backward). In the profiled step the loop body (`loop_dynamic_slice_fusion` = the `w[:, v_start:v_end]` slice, `gemm_fusion_dot_*`, online-softmax `loop_add_fusion`) each fire **32,064×**; non-collective "other" op count is **173,216**.
- **Fix (`63a90b9fc`):** drop the hard batch-minimum; activate on large vocab (`V ≥ 65536`, the real memory driver) and tile by `min(B, 8192)`. Per-device 4096 now runs as one full-vocab GEMM; larger batches still tile to bound peak logits memory. Tests updated; lint + pyrefly clean.
- **Result delta:** training mean MFU **9.51 → 12.6–13.1** (now the fastest CE; `xla` 12.57); "other" op count **173,216 → 14,160**. Standalone microbench at per-device 4096: **−52% → +31%** vs `xla` (the kernel is fine in isolation — reproduces #6596's "GEMM-bound near roofline"; the regression was purely the activation gate vs the sharded batch).
- **Confidence:** replicated (training 3×; standalone gate-sweep 3× at per-device 4096/8192/32768).
- **Ruled out:** `--xla_gpu_triton_gemm_any=false` (fragmentation persists as cuBLAS, MFU flat); missing LM-head sharding (`main` already applies `Plm_head`); jax/jaxlib version (identical 0.10.0).
- **Secondary (single-node MFU after the fix):** reliable ceiling ≈ **14.8 MFU** (b16 / per-device 8192 = max fitting batch; b20/b24/b32 OOM). `--xla_gpu_enable_latency_hiding_scheduler=true` is a real ~+16% lever but adds ~30 GiB peak that only fits reliably at b8 (→14.6); at b16 it OOMs (fit 1 of 4 → NCCL hang; `cuda_malloc_async` no help). The original June ~16 reliably needs a memory/transport change (selective remat, MoE transport #6597, or multi-node), not single-node tuning.

issues.body:
## Description
`ResourceConfig.with_tpu([...])` can only express TPU alternatives that share both `vm_count` and `chips_per_vm` (`lib/fray/src/fray/types.py:354`). Iris enforces the same shape constraint when validating `device-variant IN` candidates (`lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/constraints.py:720`).

This blocks valid capacity-fallback requests such as "any single-host TPU under 16 chips". Today callers must split that into separate jobs or worker pools:

- `v5litepod-1`, `v6e-1`
- `v4-8`, `v5p-8`, `v5litepod-4`, `v6e-4`
- `v5litepod-8`, `v6e-8`

The limitation is the request encoding: one primary TPU shape plus a `device_variant IN (...)` constraint. A richer resource-union representation could let each candidate carry its own full shape, e.g. `(variant, chips_per_vm, vm_count, replicas)`.

### Definition of Done
- Fray/Iris can represent heterogeneous TPU alternatives without relying on one primary shape.
- Iris validates and schedules each candidate using its own topology.
- Existing same-shape `with_tpu([...])` behavior keeps working.
- Tests cover mixed 1-chip, 4-chip, and 8-chip single-host TPU alternatives.

issues.author: ravwojdyla
issues.body:
* MATES: https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.06046 
* Group-MATES paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.14709

We would like to understand if we could employ data selection as opposed to RegMix based data mixing.

If we could pull it off there would be a number of advantages:
* online data selection that adapts to the model
* replaces offline mixture sweeps with online influence estimation
* doesn't require brittle quality/domain bucketing

There's a number of experiment we would need to run to evaluate the feasibility, including:
* can we use ICL to approximate the gradient-step/influence
* how important is it to compute pairwise influence (i.e. group vs global ranking)
* per-example influence selection at fixed compute beats random/RegMix

comments.author: ravwojdyla-agent
comments.body:
🤖 Early results from a first pass at the **ICL-as-influence** question (key question #1), plus an over-time influence study. Posting findings so far; the gradient-oracle validation is still running.

## Setup
- **Model/run:** `adamh-scaling-ladder-nemotron-optimal-1e+23` (~25B, Qwen3/Llama-arch), 8 HF checkpoints (steps 10k…70k, 74883).
- **Reference probe `D_r` = GPQA-diamond** (198 items); probe loss = NLL of the gold answer + explanation conditioned on the question.
- **Candidate units = the 9 `nemotron_mix` components** (quality×kind); ran the 7 Nemotron buckets (`hq_actual, hq_synth, medium_high, medium, medium_low, low_actual, low_synth`), 64 docs each.
- **ICL-influence** (the cheap signal, forward-only): `i(x) = L(D_r | neutral-ctx) − L(D_r | x-in-context)` — does *conditioning* on a doc lower GPQA loss, contrastive vs a fixed neutral control (to subtract the generic "any context" effect).
- Code: `experiments/mates_icl/` · data + plots: `gs://marin-us-central2/rav/mates_icl/`.

## Q1 — can ICL approximate gradient-step influence? ⏳ in progress
Building the gradient oracle `⟨∇L_GPQA(θ), ∇L_bucket(θ)⟩` (MATES first-order influence) at steps 10k & 74883 to Spearman-correlate against the ICL ranking. Code works + CPU-validated; the run is **blocked on TPU scheduling** (interactive jobs starved by production gang jobs in us-central2). Will update with the correlation.

## Q2 — does influence ranking change over training? ✅ yes
ICL-influence bucket **rank** over checkpoints (1 = most influential for GPQA):
```
bucket         10k  20k  30k  40k  50k  60k  70k  74883
hq_actual       3    2    3    2    1    2    1    1
medium_high     1    3    1    3    2    1    2    2
low_actual      2    1    2    1    4    3    3    4
medium          5    5    4    5    3    4    5    3
medium_low      4    4    5    4    5    5    4    5
hq_synth        6    6    6    6    6    6    6    6
low_synth       7    7    7    7    7    7    7    7
```
- **Synthetic data is least influential for GPQA at every checkpoint** (`low_synth` rank 7, `hq_synth` rank 6 — rock stable). Real extracted web text dominates the top.
- **Ranking is checkpoint-dependent** — `hq_actual` rises to #1 by late training; `low_actual` drifts from top-tier early → mid-pack late. This supports MATES's founding premise that influence is *local* (→ dynamic selection should beat static).
- Influence magnitudes shrink toward 0 over training (in-context docs perturb a stronger model less).

## Bonus — does the *nature* of influential docs change?
Scored all 448 docs once (LLM, 0–10 "graduate-science intellectual richness"; corpus mean 2.18) and tracked `Spearman(influence, richness)` per checkpoint:
```
step    10k    20k    30k    40k    50k    60k    70k   74883
rho    0.054  0.061  0.020 -0.068  0.118  0.050  0.097  0.166
```
Weak but **increasing**: early, intellectual richness is ~uncorrelated with influence; by the final checkpoint it's a (modest) positive predictor. Risers early→late are science/reasoning content (a quantum-computing explainer, CS problem-solving, a neuroscience finding); fallers are generic web boilerplate (shoe repair, drug-store listings, product copy). **Caveat:** at the very top of the per-doc list the signal is noisy and generic fluent text persists — the shift is an aggregate reweighting, not a clean flip.

Plots: `ranking_over_time.png`, `interest_trend.png` under `gs://marin-us-central2/rav/mates_icl/`.

## Caveats
- Per-document ICL influence is noisy; the clean signal is at bucket level.
- ICL-specific confound: in-context influence can be inflated by lexical overlap ("copying" from context) vs a true gradient step — partly controlled via the neutral baseline + overlap checks.
- GPQA-specific reference; coarse bucket granularity; **no closed-loop selection+retrain yet** (the real feasibility gate — select by influence, continue-pretrain, compare to random/RegMix at equal compute).

comments.author: ravwojdyla-agent
comments.body:
🤖 **Online (dynamic, per-document) selection results — and a positive validation.**

Following the static closed-loop (which found influence-weighted *mixtures* don't beat the default diverse mix), I built the more MATES-faithful **staged online loop** (`experiments/mates_icl/online_select.py`): train a small LM, and at each stage re-score a candidate pool with the *current* model (model-aware ICL-influence), select the next stage's data per-document, train, repeat. Methods: `random` (control), `topk` (MATES), `diverse` (Group-MATES, n-gram redundancy penalty), all forked from the same init. Metric = GPQA-probe NLL (nats/token, lower = better).

## Headline: done right, influence selection beats random — reproducibly

Setup: 50M Llama, 14k-doc Nemotron pool, warm-started to competence then 5 selection stages, **consume-once** (no re-picking), 2 seeds.

```
final probe NLL   random    topk(MATES)   diverse(Group-MATES)
seed 0            7.527       7.587          7.491
seed 1            7.565       7.530          7.533
```
Across both seeds × 5 stages: **`diverse` beats `random` 10/10 stage-comparisons, `topk` 9/10.** Effect modest (~0.05–0.13 nats ≈ a few % perplexity) but consistent and reproducible.

## The arc — earlier negatives were methodological artifacts

| experiment | result | cause |
|---|---|---|
| static grug-MoE mixture selection | loses to random | narrowing the mix collapses diversity |
| dynamic, **from-scratch** init, re-picking | ties random (~7.8) | random-init model → meaningless influence; re-picking same docs → overfit (topk train_loss collapsed 5.2→2.8, probe degraded to 7.97) |
| dynamic, **warm-start + consume-once** | **beats random ✓** | competent model → real signal; fresh data each stage → no overfit |

So the cheap ICL proxy only carries signal under the conditions MATES actually operates in:
1. **Competent model** — influence from a near-random model is noise; score on an already-pretraining model.
2. **Consume-once / diversity-aware** — re-selecting the same top docs overfits; this is also why **Group-MATES (diverse) ≥ MATES (top-k)** throughout.

## Validation caveats (honest scope)
- Directional validation of the *mechanism*, not a production-scale proof.
- Tiny: 50M model, GPQA probe (a 50M model barely does GPQA → low SNR); modest ~0.1-nat effect; 2 seeds.
- Bucket-level ICL↔gradient-oracle correlation was weak/divergent (n=7), but the per-doc signal works in the closed loop — the bucket test was just underpowered.

## Next to harden
1. Scale model (d1024+) and pool — effect should grow as the model can actually use the data.
2. Swap the gradient oracle (or a trained predictor) in as the proxy; compare to ICL.
3. More seeds + a held-out science eval for significance.

Artifacts: `experiments/mates_icl/` (`score_icl.py`, `oracle_influence.py`, `online_select.py`, `launch_selection.py`, analysis/plots); data + results under `gs://marin-us-central2/rav/mates_icl/`.

comments.author: ravwojdyla-agent
comments.body:
🤖 **Scaling result: the cheap-proxy selection advantage grows with model + pool size (and it reproduces).**

Building on the online-loop validation (warm-start + consume-once → influence selection beats random), I scaled the model d512 → d1024 → d3200 (~3B) and the pool 14k → 50k docs, hill-climbing the metric **ΔNLL = probe_nll(random) − probe_nll(selected)** (GPQA-probe, nats/token, seed-averaged, at matched compute).

## The scaling ladder

```
config        final-stage ΔNLL (rand−diverse)   rand−topk   warmed-base NLL
d512  / 14k          +0.040                         —            ~7.5
d1024 / 50k          +0.052                         —             6.85
d3200 / 50k          +0.089                       +0.135          6.41
```

- **Monotonic growth**: the advantage more than doubles from d512 to d3200 (+0.04 → +0.089 diverse, +0.135 top-k).
- **Reproducible**: d3200 across 3 seeds, all positive (rand−diverse +0.062 / +0.151 / +0.055).
- **Stable**: at d3200, `topk`/`diverse` beat `random` at *every* stage — no overfitting collapse — and the base model keeps improving (NLL 7.5 → 6.41).

This is the key signal: the payoff *increases* with scale, i.e. it is **not** a small-model artifact. d3200 trajectory:
```
stage   random   topk    diverse
0       6.409    6.409   6.409   (competent warmed base)
1       6.610    6.469   6.452
2       6.559    6.424   6.462
3       6.584    6.440   6.454
4       6.538    6.449   6.476
```

## What it took (now baked into `experiments/mates_icl/online_select.py`)
The earlier all-negative results were methodological artifacts. The cheap ICL proxy only carries signal under conditions intrinsic to how MATES operates:
1. **Warm-start to competence** — influence from a random-init model is noise; warmup must *scale with model size* (500 steps undertrained 3B → 1500 fixed it: base 7.32 → 6.41).
2. **Consume-once selection** — re-picking the same top docs overfits (topk train_loss collapsed 5.2→2.8, probe degraded).
3. **Per-stage candidate subsample scoring** (`score_pool_sample`) — score a sample, not the whole pool, each stage; ~3× faster *and* more MATES-faithful.

## Notable: at scale, plain top-k ≥ diversity-aware
At d3200 **`topk` (MATES) > `diverse` (Group-MATES)** (+0.135 vs +0.089) — once consume-once + subsample scoring already supply cross-stage diversity, the extra n-gram diversity penalty is unnecessary and slightly costs influence. Group-MATES helped at small scale (homogeneous selection); plain top-k wins once diversity is otherwise handled.

## Honest scope
~3B model, GPQA probe, ICL proxy (not the gradient oracle); modest-but-growing absolute effect (~0.09–0.14 nats ≈ ~10–14% perplexity at the final stage, larger mid-trajectory). Not yet frontier-scale or a head-to-head vs RegMix.

## Next
- Continue the ladder (bigger pool / larger model) — does ΔNLL keep climbing?
- Swap the gradient oracle (or a trained predictor) in as the proxy and compare to ICL.
- The decision-relevant comparison: influence-selection vs a tuned **RegMix** mixture at equal compute.

## Summary

This experiment measures whether chunked MoE routing improves serving throughput enough to offset the BPB gap seen in the trained 1B/100B-token chunked-MoE baselines. It isolates the architecture effect with random-initialized d2048, d2560, and d3200 models, comparing token, chunk4, chunk8, and chunk16 routing across long-prefill/short-decode and short-prefill/long-decode regimes. Early single-pass d2048 results suggested chunking can improve 32k-prefill throughput while leaving decode roughly unchanged, but the first benchmark attempts also exposed batch-1 MoE sharding issues and were superseded. The active run is now the 72-child repeated-timing sweep under `/pc0618/chunked-moe-inf-random-v5p32-warm3-20260618`; final conclusions should wait for that run instead of relying on the partial v5 table.

## Description

Current chunked-MoE training results suggest chunked routing improves throughput but leaves a validation BPB gap. The next question is serving behavior: chunked routing should mostly help prefill, while decode should remain similar if the cached-expert/sliding decode path is efficient and keeps token-level decode semantics.

This issue tracks a random-model inference throughput sweep so we can measure the architectural throughput effect without waiting for trained checkpoints at every scale.

Chunked routing should improve prefill throughput increasingly with chunk size, especially at long ISL, while decode throughput should remain close to token routing if the cached-expert/sliding decode implementation avoids extra per-token routing overhead. ## Summary

This issue tracks the chunked MoE routing experiment for Grug MoE models. The core idea is to reduce router/top-k and routing-metadata pressure by assigning a single routing decision to a chunk of tokens rather than routing every token independently. The experiment compares token-level routing against chunked routing with chunk sizes 4, 8, and 16.

The current implementation family uses causal chunk routing for prefill/training: each chunk route is derived from causal context rather than future tokens, so the routing decision remains compatible with autoregressive training. Decode is handled separately because ordinary autoregressive generation advances one live token per step; the current sliding-window decode path still dispatches one token at a time.

## Why this can save systems cost

### Prefill / training

In normal token routing, each MoE layer routes approximately `B * S` positions:

- Router GEMM: `[B*S, D] @ [D, E]`
- Top-k: over `[B*S, E]`
- Routing metadata / sorting / group-size bookkeeping: token granularity
- Permute/unpermute: token granularity

With chunked routing of size `C`, routing decisions shrink to approximately `B * S / C`:

- Router GEMM becomes `[B*S/C, D] @ [D, E]`
- Top-k is over `[B*S/C, E]`
- Dispatch metadata can be generated at chunk granularity
- Permute/unpermute bookkeeping can reduce by roughly `C` if the implementation dispatches chunks as routing units or otherwise reuses chunk-level expert assignments

Important caveat: expert FFN compute is not reduced if all tokens are still evaluated by the selected experts. The expected savings are router/top-k, sort/grouping, dispatch metadata, and potentially lower permute/unpermute overhead/fragmentation. The all-to-all payload may not shrink unless the dispatch representation itself becomes chunked or avoids per-token movement.

### Decode

Decode is different because generation advances one live token per step.

- Sliding-window decode that computes router context over a window but dispatches only the current live token does not automatically reduce routing decisions by `C`; it mostly changes router context.
- Decode can amortize top-k/router work by `C` only if a routing decision is cached/reused across `C` decode steps or the decode API batches multiple future tokens/MTP-style positions.
- Even with cached routing, expert FFN work and KV-cache attention remain per generated token, so absolute decode speedups may be smaller than prefill speedups unless routing/permutation is a large fraction of step time.
- Reusing routing metadata across decode steps can reduce top-k and permute/unpermute bookkeeping, but it introduces a stronger semantic choice than sliding-window-only decode.

## Metric definitions

- `BPB` is the token-weighted/micro-average bits-per-byte over the validation mixture. Large datasets or datasets with more evaluated bytes contribute more to the aggregate.
- `macro BPB` first computes BPB per tagged validation dataset and then averages across datasets. Each dataset gets equal weight, so this is more sensitive to broad cross-domain degradation.

## Corrected validation results

These results are from the corrected full-validation jobs for the latest learned top-k/load-balanced `1p5top8lb-useast5` checkpoints. The validation config matches the latest training policy: `plain_topk`, `causal_start`, `force_uniform_routing=false`, `router_z_loss_coef=0.001`, and `router_load_balancing_loss_coef=0.01`.

| run | full eval loss | macro loss | BPB | macro BPB |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| token | 3.1352 | 3.3033 | 1.0820 | 1.1586 |
| chunk4 | 3.1780 | 3.3583 | 1.0958 | 1.1774 |
| chunk8 | 3.1999 | 3.3757 | 1.1033 | 1.1834 |
| chunk16 | 3.2177 | 3.4065 | 1.1094 | 1.1941 |

Interpretation: unlike the earlier uniform-routing validation suite, the corrected learned top-k causal-start setup shows a clear validation tradeoff. Chunking improves training throughput but worsens validation as chunk size increases. On macro BPB, chunk4 is `+0.0188`, chunk8 is `+0.0248`, and chunk16 is `+0.0354` worse than token routing.

## W&B provenance

Corrected full-validation runs:

- token: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/chunked_perf_full_validation_token_ring-1p5top8lb-useast5-fullval99k
- chunk4: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/chunked_perf_full_validation_chunk4_ring-1p5top8lb-useast5-fullval99k
- chunk8: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/chunked_perf_full_validation_chunk8_ring-1p5top8lb-useast5-fullval99k
- chunk16: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/chunked_perf_full_validation_chunk16_ring-1p5top8lb-useast5-fullval99k

Corresponding completed training runs:

- token: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/chunked_perf_train_eval_small_token_learned_plain_topk_causal_start_rz0p001_lb0p01_ring-1p5top8lb-useast5
- chunk4: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/chunked_perf_train_eval_small_chunk4_learned_plain_topk_causal_start_rz0p001_lb0p01_ring-1p5top8lb-useast5
- chunk8: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/chunked_perf_train_eval_small_chunk8_learned_plain_topk_causal_start_rz0p001_lb0p01_ring-1p5top8lb-useast5
- chunk16: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/chunked_perf_train_eval_small_chunk16_learned_plain_topk_causal_start_rz0p001_lb0p01_ring-1p5top8lb-useast5

## Next steps

1. Profile prefill with token vs chunk4/chunk8/chunk16 and break out router GEMM, top-k, sort/group-size metadata, permute, unpermute, all-to-all, and expert FFN time.
2. Separate decode experiments into sliding-window-context decode versus cached/reused-route decode, because only the latter should reduce routing decisions over decode steps.
3. Confirm whether the implementation dispatches chunks as chunk units or still expands back to token-level dispatch metadata, since that determines whether permute/unpermute savings are actually realized.
4. Investigate whether less aggressive chunking, auxiliary router supervision, or distillation can recover the validation gap while preserving some prefill throughput savings.

The `datakit-nemotron` weekly ferry failed when the `verify_fuzzy_dups` step raised a bare `TimeoutError`, which `StepRunner` surfaced as `RuntimeError: 1 step(s) failed`. Five of seven stages completed (download → normalize → minhash → fuzzy_dups); verify never loaded its in-memory document store, so `consolidate` and `tokenize` never ran.

The verify stage sizes its worker pool to `min(len(shards), 1000) = 1000` workers, each requesting `cpu=16, ram=160g` (`experiments/ferries/datakit_nemotron_ferry.py:160`, `verify_fuzzy_dups.py:817`). Unlike the earlier pull-based stages, `verify_fuzzy_dups` blocks on the **entire** pool becoming ready before loading the store, because the store is hash-partitioned across every worker:

```
verify_fuzzy_dups.py:835  document_store = ctx.load_memory_store(...)
context.py:398            coordinator.worker_handles.remote(pool.worker_count, ready_timeout).result(timeout=ready_timeout)
```

`ready_timeout` is `1800`s (`FUZZY_VERIFICATION_STORE_CONFIG.ready_timeout`). In eu-west4 the pool reached only ~133 of 1000 workers ready (~06:15) and stayed flat for 25 minutes; the wait hit its 1800s deadline at 06:40:39 and raised `TimeoutError`. The earlier stages tolerated a partial pool: `minhash` (64 GB workers) had 490/538 workers succeed and the stage completed. Only verify requires the full gang simultaneously, so it is the stage that capacity pressure breaks.

The ferry and verify code were not changed for this run (HEAD is a dependency bump, #8939), so this is environmental capacity pressure exposing a fragile design: a 1000-worker, 160 GB-RAM pool with an all-or-nothing readiness barrier and a 30-minute timeout cannot survive slow autoscaling.

- op1, own recipe: 4.1686 / 3.7217 / 3.5456 / 3.4738

## What replicates

- **The transfer probe.** Operator-1 under the vanilla recipe beats plain vanilla by −0.0100 (paper: −0.0144). The K=1 boundary operator architecture is neutral-to-slightly-positive at this scale, matching the paper's direction and magnitude.
- **Absolute scale.** Our vanilla is 0.06 below the paper's number — expected given the documented deviations (FineWeb 10BT slice vs the full corpus, sequence packing without cross-doc attention masking, modded-nanogpt Muon internals, decoupled WD on the AdamW groups only, TPU vs the paper's H100s).

## What does not replicate

- **The paper's central claim for Operator-1**: own-recipe 3.3057 < vanilla 3.3279 (−0.022). We get the opposite sign at 10× the magnitude: own-recipe 3.4738 = **+0.208** vs our vanilla. The arm is behind from the first eval (4.17 vs 3.74 at step 500) and the gap never closes — a hyperparameter-configuration effect, not a training collapse.
- The recipe transcription was verified against paper Table 5 three separate times (most recently against the paper source): GLR 0.04, ELRM 0.905, HLRM 0.08, RM 0.5, OM 1, α<sub>emb</sub> 1, WD 0.05, WTE 0.113, UIS 0.354, WU 0, WDR 0.8, β 0.8/0.98, ε 1e-10. The LR schedule was verified step-by-step: constant GLR from step 0 (the paper specifies no warmup for Operator-1), linear warmdown over the last 80% to zero.

## Interpretation

Consistent with the Phase-0 MoE ablation (#9280): the boundary-operator architecture does not carry a robust gain in our stack, and the paper's Operator-1 advantage is not robust to the documented implementation deviations. The own-recipe inversion (paper −0.008 recipe benefit → our +0.218 penalty) points at recipe–implementation interactions — most plausibly WU=0 with full GLR 0.04 under our Muon, or the WTE/UIS/ELRM init-scale cluster — which the paper's reported numbers do not disambiguate. A knob-at-a-time ablation of the Operator-1 recipe under our implementation would isolate it (not done here).

**Attribution: the model-side init cluster is the driver.**

- **Warmup is eliminated.** `screen-wu0` is indistinguishable from base (no-warmup at full GLR 0.04 is harmless under the vanilla recipe), and `screen-own-wu40` stays fully broken — restoring warmup does not repair the own recipe. The top suspect going in is out.

issues.body:
tl;dr

PivotRL (https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.21383) is a flavor of RL that was used extensively in Nemotron-Ultra post-training. It operates on existing SFT trajectories to combine the compute efficiency of SFT with the OOD accuracy of E2E RL. PivotRL first executes local, on-policy rollouts and filters for pivots: informative intermediate turns where sampled actions exhibit high variance in outcomes; then it utilizes rewards for functional-equivalent actions rather than demanding strict string matching with the SFT data demonstration.

MarinSkyRL training data resolves to two kinds, a plain directory (`ArtifactDataSource`) and a TaskTrove parquet cohort (`TaskTroveDataSource`). Neither carries per-step annotations.

Scope: a Marin data source that resolves per-step pivot annotations with artifact identity, request plumbing for them, and a `MARIN_SKYRL` pin bump (`lib/marin/src/marin/external_dependencies.py:73`) to a MarinSkyRL revision that consumes the annotations and applies step weights in the training loop.

Open questions:

- Compute pivot scores (teacher-forced NLL under the student) as a Marin
  artifact step, or accept only precomputed annotations?
- Carry detection parameters (spike threshold, pivot weight) as named
  `SkyRLSpec` fields or leave them to `config_yaml` and `overrides`?

Done when:

- A pivot-annotated source resolves to a `ResolvedDataSource` whose
  identity covers the annotations, so the step fingerprint changes when
  annotations change.
- `SkyRLLaunchRequest` carries the annotations, and the pinned MarinSkyRL
  commit applies non-uniform step weights end to end.
- Annotation-free specs keep today's fingerprints and training behavior.
- `tests/rl/test_skyrl.py` covers the new source kind and request fields.
- We can reproduce this result from the paper E2E in MarinSkyRL -> 'On GSM8K (200 problems, 182 Kimi K2.5 competition-math traces, Gemma 4 E4B student), pivot-weighted SFT at 2.5x loss scored 80.0% vs 74.5% for uniform SFT against an 85.5% base."

issues.body:
Picks up **item 6 (Basic numeracy failure modes)** of #7090.

This sub-issue scopes the eval design for adding a NUPA / Number Cookbook direct numeracy benchmark to Marin.

## Goal

Add a runnable **NUPA / Number Cookbook direct numeracy eval** to Marin so models can be evaluated on basic numeric-processing failure modes beyond existing broad math benchmarks.

NUPA is a good fit for item 6 because it evaluates deterministic numeric tasks across number representations and digit lengths:

- integer, float, fraction, scientific notation
- arithmetic, comparison, digit-level operations, format conversion
- metrics that expose partial numeric failures, not just final exact accuracy

## Dataset

Candidate source dataset:

https://huggingface.co/datasets/HaotongYang/NUPA_text

Original paper:

https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.03766

The released HF dataset is MIT-licensed and contains `train`, `valid`, and `test` splits. The files are nested by task and digit length, so Marin / lm-eval-harness likely needs a preprocessing step that flattens them into row-per-example records.

Source shape:

```json
{
  "max_Float_Float_Float": {
    "3": [
      "Directly return the answer as a float without any comma separator, like 10.4 . Get the maximal number: 9.11 and 9.9 = 9.9"
    ]
  }
}
```

Flattened eval record:

```json
{
  "task_name": "max_Float_Float_Float",
  "operation": "max",
  "number_type": "Float",
  "digit": 3,
  "bucket": "S",
  "prompt": "Directly return the answer as a float without any comma separator, like 10.4 . Get the maximal number: 9.11 and 9.9 =",
  "answer": "9.9",
  "answer_format": "float"
}
```

The flattened representation should be suitable for deterministic loading, task filtering, and per-bucket metric reporting.

## Proposed scope

Add NUPA as a direct numeracy eval in Marin with:

- task / representation coverage
- digit-length metadata
- per-task and per-digit-bucket reporting
- deterministic construction from the released `test` split

## Metrics

Match the original NUPA paper's core metrics with clean-room Marin/lm-eval code:

- `exact_match`: normalized prediction exactly matches the gold answer
- `digit_match`: fraction of matching digits by numeric component
- `dlength`: absolute difference in digit length

Likely useful additional metric:

- `format_valid_rate`: prediction has the required output format, e.g. integer, float, fraction, scientific notation

Do not vendor scoring code from the Number Cookbook GitHub repo, because that repo is GPL-3.0. Use the MIT HF dataset and implement a small clean-room scorer from the paper's metric definitions.

## Integration approach

Preferred direction: integrate as an **lm-eval-harness generation task**, not as a new standalone evaluator.

The task implementation should include:

- local lm-eval task YAMLs
- custom Python metrics
- any Marin / Levanter wiring needed for the tasks to be discoverable and runnable

Rough shape:

```text
experiments/evals/lm_eval_tasks/nupa/
  README.md
  nupa_add_integer.yaml
  nupa_max_float.yaml
  ...
  metrics.py
  utils.py
```

Then expose the tasks from Marin's eval config, e.g. a `NUMERACY_TASKS` or `NUPA_TASKS` tuple in `experiments/evals/task_configs.py`.

## Acceptance criteria

- A reproducible preprocessing script or documented dataset construction process for flattened NUPA eval data.
- Flattened row-per-example data suitable for lm-eval-harness, plus a tiny fixture/smoke split for tests if useful.
- Custom metric tests for exact match, digit match, dlength, and format validity.
- Runnable Marin eval tasks covering the selected NUPA task families.
- Results include per-task and per-digit-bucket metrics so failures are diagnosable.

## Overview

What is this document? This document is an attempt to formalize Marin’s policy towards what constitutes reportable, public-facing, canonical eval results for Marin models as well as the baselines we compare against.

Why do we need this document? With the first “snowball” cool-down, Marin is entering a regime where we regularly compare Marin models to existing open and closed-source models. Because Marin’s unique claim is that we are open development, we will need to hold ourselves to a high standard of transparency on how we report eval scores of Marin models and what claims we make about Marin model capabilities based on those scores.

What is in scope for this document? This document is intended to act as a living snapshot, trustworthy for any given period in time, as to the what and the how of Marin’s canonical set of evals, a set of standards to which we will aspire to hold ourselves. By "the what", we mean “which evals did we run, with what consistent set of hyperparameters and experimental constraints”. By "the how", we mean “where is the self-contained codebase that is both necessary and sufficient to reproduce our eval results independently”.

## Previous version notes

* Released Aug 4, 2026: included 11 Evalchemy benchmarks, 14 lm-eval-harness tasks, 7 Harbor agentic evals and 5 AA-II component benchmarks named as weighting targets but not run directly

Evalchemy ran against a server configured for 73,728 tokens. Marin reserves a 64-token transport
margin, yielding the 73,664-token evaluator allowance shown above; MMLU-Pro has a stricter

tokens and model output to 8,192 tokens.

`SimpleQA mini-200` and `DS-1000 mini-200` are fixed seed-42 random samples of their full
registry datasets. Harbor records the selected task names and immutable source revisions in
`simpleqa@mini-200` and `ds-1000@mini-200`; every model must use the same 200 tasks.

### Out of Distribution

* AAII 4.3

### How do we handle in-distribution and out-of-distribution evals?

#### IN-DISTRIBUTION

**We will** -- dedup against our SFT data, look at model scores while we develop the model, inspect the correlation of our ID evals with our OOD evals

**We may** -- develop synthetic RL tasks modeled on specific tasks in ID evals

**We will not** -- train on teacher rollouts from eval questions, use our ID eval instructions directly as the basis of RL data

#### OUT-OF-DISTRIBUTION

**We will** -- de-dup against our SFT raw data, look at meta-data about these evals (e.g., how big they are, general knowledge domain, etc), eval baselines on these evals

**We will not** -- look at the individual questions in the evals, look at any of our own model scores from these evals until our model is frozen, model any synthetic tasks on tasks in the evals (edited)

### Metric definitions

- **Accuracy:** the number of scored examples whose configured grader or verifier returns a correct outcome, divided by the number of scored examples. This includes exact-match rate, pass@1 with one completion, and agent-task solve rate with one trial. FinanceBench and SimpleQA mini-200 use an LLM judge; SimpleQA counts only `CORRECT` as correct, while `INCORRECT` and `NOT_ATTEMPTED` both score zero. For `piqa` and `openbookqa`, the selected answer is the option with the highest length-normalized log-likelihood (`acc_norm` in lm-eval-harness), and accuracy is the fraction of those selections that are correct. AIME24 reports the mean accuracy across its ten seeded runs.
- **CruxEval accuracy:** reported separately for input prediction and output prediction. Input prediction asks the model to reconstruct a valid function input from the code and desired output; output prediction asks it to predict the output from the code and input.
- **IFBench strict prompt-level accuracy:** the fraction of prompts for which the raw response satisfies every required constraint.
- **Mean sequence similarity:** MRCR's mean `SequenceMatcher` ratio between the response's answer span and the reference answer. A response that fails MRCR's nonce check receives zero credit.
- **Allowed context length:** This is allowed prompt + completion context length. If a model's maximum context length is less than the allowed context length, we adopt the model's maximum context length. For single-turn benchmarks, we subdivide the space into max prompt length = longest prompt in the dataset plus a bit of cushion, max response length = the remaining context window. For multi-turn benchmarks, max generation length per turn is 8192.

### Valid (Scoreable) Harbor Exceptions

For a single-step Harbor task, the following agent-terminal exceptions are valid,
scoreable outcomes when the trial also contains a completed `verifier_result`:

- `AgentTimeoutError`: the agent reached its configured execution timeout; Harbor preserves
  the work produced so far and runs the verifier.
- `ContextLengthExceededError`: the model or agent exhausted the available context; Harbor
  treats that as a classified end to the attempt and runs the verifier.
- `TurnCapExhaustedError`: the agent reached its configured turn cap without declaring
  completion; Harbor runs the verifier on the resulting state.
- `NonZeroAgentExitCodeError`: the agent process exited non-zero after potentially producing
  scoreable work; Harbor still runs the verifier. Agent-specific subclasses must be reported
  under their concrete exception type and reviewed for validity rather than silently grouped.

An exception is not sufficient evidence that a trial was scored. Include a trial in the
scoreable denominator only when `verifier_result` is present. Environment, setup, whole-trial,
artifact-collection, and verifier failures—including `AgentSetupTimeoutError`,
`EnvironmentStartTimeoutError`, `TrialTimeoutError`, `VerifierTimeoutError`,
`TrialNotScoredError`, and `VerificationNotCompletedError`—are unscored infrastructure or
harness outcomes and must be retried or reported separately. Likewise, errors such as model
authentication failures or agents killed by infrastructure are not valid model outcomes merely
because their Python classes inherit from `NonZeroAgentExitCodeError`.

## Eval launch commands (Marin)

These commands require an Iris account with access to the `marin` controller and the `cw-rno2a`
federated cluster. `MODEL_CONFIG` must be an absolute path to a Marin model-catalog YAML file whose
model and tokenizer revisions are immutable. The model must support a 73,728-token context for MRCR.
The checkout below is the public campaign revision based on the pinned Marin `main` commit above. It
adds the Evalchemy revision that correctly applies the zero-shot MMLU-Pro policy.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/marin-community/marin.git
cd marin
git checkout ba2fef7443dd5fad1b1a35402982e1c4ce71c8c0
uv sync --all-packages

export MODEL_CONFIG=/absolute/path/to/pinned-model.yaml
export TOGETHER_API_KEY="REPLACE_WITH_TOGETHER_API_KEY"
export JUDGE_API_KEY="$TOGETHER_API_KEY"
export JUDGE_BASE_URL=https://api.together.xyz/v1
export JUDGE_MODEL=openai/gpt-oss-120b

POLICY_CONFIG_DIR=$(mktemp -d)

write_chat_config() {
  config_name=$1
  task_name=$2
  runtime_extra=$3
  max_tokens=$4
  max_length=$5
  {
    echo "tasks: [$task_name]"
    echo "task_options:"
    echo "  $task_name:"
    echo "    num_fewshot: 0"
    echo "    task_alias: $config_name"
    echo "    generation: true"
    echo "apply_chat_template: true"
    echo "batch_size: 1"
    echo "seed: 42"
    echo "max_tokens: $max_tokens"
    if [ "$max_length" != "default" ]; then
      echo "max_length: $max_length"
    fi
    echo "runtime_extras: [$runtime_extra]"
  } > "$POLICY_CONFIG_DIR/$config_name.yaml"
}

write_chat_config mmlu-pro MMLUPro mmlupro 32768 65536
write_chat_config gpqa-diamond GPQADiamond gpqadiamond 32768 default
write_chat_config cruxeval CruxEval cruxeval 2048 default
write_chat_config financebench FinanceBench financebench 4096 default
write_chat_config ifbench IFBench ifbench 1024 default
write_chat_config mrcr MRCR mrcr 4096 73728

# Deterministic single-run Evalchemy and lm-eval-harness evaluations.
uv run python -m experiments.evaluation.cli launch \
  --model-config "$MODEL_CONFIG" \
  --evals math500,humanevalplus,mbppplus,olympiadbench,gsm8k-0shot,mmlu,piqa,winogrande,openbookqa,boolq,truthfulqa,triviaqa \
  --federated_cluster cw-rno2a \
  --priority interactive \
  --version eval-policy-updated

# AIME24: ten independent launches; Evalchemy generates ten responses per question in each launch.
for seed in $(seq 42 51); do
  uv run python -m experiments.evaluation.cli launch \
    --model-config "$MODEL_CONFIG" \
    --evals aime24 \
    --seed "$seed" \
    --federated_cluster cw-rno2a \
    --priority interactive \
    --version eval-policy-updated
done

# Policy additions that are not registered as named Marin eval keys at the pinned Marin commit.
uv run python -m experiments.evaluation.cli launch \
  --model-config "$MODEL_CONFIG" \
  --evalchemy-config "$POLICY_CONFIG_DIR/mmlu-pro.yaml" \
  --evalchemy-config "$POLICY_CONFIG_DIR/gpqa-diamond.yaml" \
  --evalchemy-config "$POLICY_CONFIG_DIR/cruxeval.yaml" \
  --evalchemy-config "$POLICY_CONFIG_DIR/financebench.yaml" \
  --evalchemy-config "$POLICY_CONFIG_DIR/ifbench.yaml" \
  --evalchemy-config "$POLICY_CONFIG_DIR/mrcr.yaml" \
  --federated_cluster cw-rno2a \
  --priority interactive \
  --version eval-policy-updated

# The campaign's five Harbor policies are pinned on its public experiment branch.
for config_name in swebench-recovery ot-tblite-recovery tb2-recovery simpleqa-recovery ds-1000-local; do
  curl -fsSL \
    "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/8aa9a354d30abbda89a7756e11c1a37037aa8a65/experiments/evaluation/configs/harbor/$config_name.yaml" \
    -o "experiments/evaluation/configs/harbor/$config_name.yaml"
done

# Select the policy's deterministic seed-42 mini datasets from the pinned Harbor registry.
export HARBOR_REGISTRY_URL=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/harbor/7b18505a56e5624f55887e3b20f4de452f698a7a/registry.json
uv run python - "$HARBOR_REGISTRY_URL" <<'PY'
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import yaml

registry_url = sys.argv[1]
config_dir = Path("experiments/evaluation/configs/harbor")
for filename, dataset_name in (
    ("simpleqa-recovery.yaml", "simpleqa"),
    ("ds-1000-local.yaml", "ds-1000"),
):
    path = config_dir / filename
    policy = yaml.safe_load(path.read_text())
    policy["datasets"] = [
        {
            "name": dataset_name,
            "version": "mini-200",
            "registry_url": registry_url,
        }
    ]
    if dataset_name == "ds-1000":
        # DS-1000's registry tasks must build their pinned Dockerfiles; no
        # published prebuilt image is available for this dataset version.
        policy.setdefault("environment", {})["force_build"] = True
    path.write_text(yaml.safe_dump(policy, sort_keys=False))
PY

uv run python -m experiments.evaluation.cli launch \
  --model-config "$MODEL_CONFIG" \
  --harbor-config experiments/evaluation/configs/harbor/swebench-recovery.yaml \
  --harbor-config experiments/evaluation/configs/harbor/ot-tblite-recovery.yaml \
  --harbor-config experiments/evaluation/configs/harbor/tb2-recovery.yaml \
  --harbor-config experiments/evaluation/configs/harbor/simpleqa-recovery.yaml \
  --harbor-config experiments/evaluation/configs/harbor/ds-1000-local.yaml \
  --federated_cluster cw-rno2a \
  --priority interactive \
  --version eval-policy-updated
```

## Eval launch commands (Standalone)

The standalone path requires an OpenAI-compatible endpoint reachable from both the local evaluator
and Daytona sandboxes. `MODEL_BASE_URL` is the API root ending in `/v1`; `MODEL_ID` must match the
model name returned by its `/models` endpoint; and `TOKENIZER_ID` must be an immutable Hugging Face
model or tokenizer revision. Evalchemy executes generated code for HumanEvalPlus and MBPPPlus.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy.git
cd evalchemy
git checkout 65c80022b8be98012a4ce6cd98a5168a7a58d99e
uv sync --python 3.12 --extra benchmarks --extra serve-eval

export MODEL_BASE_URL=https://example-model-endpoint.invalid/v1
export MODEL_ID="REPLACE_WITH_SERVED_MODEL_NAME"
export MODEL_API_KEY="REPLACE_WITH_MODEL_ENDPOINT_API_KEY"
export TOKENIZER_ID="REPLACE_WITH_HUGGING_FACE_TOKENIZER_ID"
export TOKENIZER_REVISION="REPLACE_WITH_IMMUTABLE_TOKENIZER_REVISION"
export TOGETHER_API_KEY="REPLACE_WITH_TOGETHER_API_KEY"
export JUDGE_API_KEY="$TOGETHER_API_KEY"
export JUDGE_BASE_URL=https://api.together.xyz/v1
export JUDGE_MODEL=openai/gpt-oss-120b

mkdir -p results/evalchemy

run_chat_eval() {
  task_name=$1
  num_fewshot=$2
  max_tokens=$3
  max_length=$4
  seed=$5
  output_name=$6
  shift 6
  uv run eval \
    --model local-chat-completions \
    --model_args "model=$MODEL_ID,base_url=${MODEL_BASE_URL%/}/chat/completions,api_key=$MODEL_API_KEY,tokenizer=$TOKENIZER_ID,revision=$TOKENIZER_REVISION,tokenizer_backend=huggingface,tokenized_requests=False,num_concurrent=32,max_retries=8,timeout=1800,max_length=$max_length" \
    --tasks "$task_name" \
    --num_fewshot "$num_fewshot" \
    --batch_size 1 \
    --seed "$seed" \
    --max_length "$max_length" \
    --max_tokens "$max_tokens" \
    --gen_kwargs "max_gen_toks=$max_tokens" \
    --apply_chat_template \
    --log_samples \
    --output_path "results/evalchemy/$output_name" \
    "$@"
}

run_completion_eval() {
  task_name=$1
  num_fewshot=$2
  max_tokens=$3
  max_length=$4
  uv run eval \
    --model local-completions \
    --model_args "model=$MODEL_ID,base_url=${MODEL_BASE_URL%/}/completions,api_key=$MODEL_API_KEY,tokenizer=$TOKENIZER_ID,revision=$TOKENIZER_REVISION,tokenizer_backend=huggingface,tokenized_requests=False,num_concurrent=32,max_retries=8,timeout=1800,max_length=$max_length" \
    --tasks "$task_name" \
    --num_fewshot "$num_fewshot" \
    --batch_size 1 \
    --seed 42 \
    --max_length "$max_length" \
    --max_tokens "$max_tokens" \
    --gen_kwargs "max_gen_toks=$max_tokens" \
    --log_samples \
    --output_path "results/evalchemy/$task_name"
}

run_chat_eval MATH500 0 8192 73664 42 math500
for seed in $(seq 42 51); do
  run_chat_eval AIME24 0 8192 73664 "$seed" "aime24-seed-$seed"
done
run_chat_eval HumanEvalPlus 0 1024 73664 42 humanevalplus --confirm_run_unsafe_code
run_chat_eval MBPPPlus 0 1024 73664 42 mbppplus --confirm_run_unsafe_code
run_chat_eval OlympiadBench 0 32768 73664 42 olympiadbench
run_chat_eval MMLUPro 0 32768 65536 42 mmlu-pro
run_chat_eval GPQADiamond 0 32768 73664 42 gpqa-diamond
run_chat_eval CruxEval 0 2048 73664 42 cruxeval
run_chat_eval FinanceBench 0 4096 73664 42 financebench
run_chat_eval IFBench 0 1024 73664 42 ifbench
run_chat_eval MRCR 0 4096 73664 42 mrcr

run_completion_eval gsm8k 0 512 73664
run_completion_eval mmlu 5 256 73664
run_completion_eval piqa 0 256 73664
run_completion_eval winogrande 5 256 73664
run_completion_eval openbookqa 0 256 73664
run_completion_eval boolq 0 256 73664
run_completion_eval truthfulqa_mc2 0 256 73664
run_completion_eval triviaqa 5 128 73664
```

Run the Harbor evaluations from a separate directory so Harbor's environment does not share

## Standards for presenting Marin evals

* For each benchmark, plot Snowball perf, along with baseline(s) perf, on an x-y scatterplot, with y being perf and x being total training FLOPS
* Use 6ND proxy for pretraining and SFT FLOPS, and 6 * max_tokens_per_rollout / max_context_length * n_rollouts * active_params proxy for RL FLOPS
* In a separate standalone table, include all raw scores in XX.y format, with 95% confidence intervals derived from the trial count -- do not leave gaps, use table captions for results that require further context, use the exact same model family in the table as was present in the x-y scatterplot(s)
* Eval results are reportable IFF the eval in question completed with <10% of trials encountering infrastructure errors
* Eval results are reportable IFF they include provenance, in the form of model traces, and where available, verifier traces
* Any eval result that is publicly presented should clearly distinguish whether the benchmarks are in-distribution (part of the dev set), held out, or a mix of the two
* Any eval result that is publicly presented in a major release should report on *all* ID and OOD benchmarks, avoiding cherry picking, substitution, or new evals outside of a formal policy update
* For active development and internal communication, it is fine to define working subsets of the ID benchmarks and report on those in isolation

## Future considerations

* We would like to post-train multiple Snowball checkpoints, experimenting with different degrees of compute applied to post-training, to establish trade-off lines / domains
* We would like to think about a "marin model card" that would set minimum standards for true open development

comments.body:
🤖 **Status:** Analysis only — this is a multi-module feature (issue template + nightly automation + doc/blog generation), larger than a self-contained fix, so handing back a proposed approach for human review before implementation.

# Research

Most of the requested machinery already exists in pieces; the gap is a GitHub-native experiment template, a generation step that turns reaped issues into newcomer-facing docs/teasers, and a workflow that actually runs the nightly reap on schedule.

**Relevant code**
- [`.agents/skills/scrub-experiment-issue-tldrs/SKILL.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/.agents/skills/scrub-experiment-issue-tldrs/SKILL.md) — already reaps `experiment` issues nightly and maintains `<!-- experiment-tldr:start/end -->` summary blocks. Has `schedule_cron: "0 8 * * *"` but it is **not wired to anything**.
- [`infra/pre-commit.py#L718-L724`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/pre-commit.py#L718-L724) — the *only* consumer of `schedule_cron`/`schedule_tz`: it validates them, nothing executes them.
- [`.github/workflows/ops-nightshift-doc-drift.yaml`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/.github/workflows/ops-nightshift-doc-drift.yaml) + [`infra/cron/nightshift_doc_drift.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/cron/nightshift_doc_drift.py) — the established "nightly agent" pattern (workflow on `cron` → script invokes `claude --model=opus` with an app token, opens PRs/issues, no self-credit).
- [`scripts/pm/itemize_experiment_issues.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/scripts/pm/itemize_experiment_issues.py) + [`.agents/skills/organize-experiments/SKILL.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/.agents/skills/organize-experiments/SKILL.md) — already harvest `experiment`-labeled issues into [`docs/reports/index.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/docs/reports/index.md), resolving W&B run names via `wandb.Api()`.
- [`.agents/skills/file-issue/SKILL.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/.agents/skills/file-issue/SKILL.md) (experiment body, ~L55-83) — the experiment issue body template (TL;DR / Hypothesis / Status / Links / Decision Log / Conclusion) lives in a skill, **not** as a GitHub form. There is no `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/` directory.

**Gaps vs. the ask:** (1) no GitHub-native experiment template so humans/agents get the structure for free; (2) the nightly reaper isn't scheduled — `schedule_cron` is decorative; (3) no step that emits concise newcomer docs / blog teasers (only TL;DR blocks on the issue itself and a link index); (4) no surface (blog / recent-experiments page) showing ongoing vs. finished + author.

# Proposed Approach

Build on what exists rather than adding a parallel system. Four increments, each independently reviewable:

1. **GitHub-native experiment template** (`.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/experiment.yml` + `config.yml`). Mirror the `file-issue` experiment body (TL;DR, Hypothesis/Goal, Status, Links: Logbook/W&B/PRs, Decision Log, Conclusion) and auto-apply the `experiment` label. This is the small, self-contained "template" piece and the natural first PR — but it should still be reviewed for field wording first. Keep `file-issue/SKILL.md` as the source of truth; the form references it.

2. **Wire the nightly reaper.** Add `.github/workflows/ops-nightshift-experiment-docs.yaml` + `infra/cron/nightshift_experiment_docs.py` following the doc-drift pattern (app token, `claude --model=opus`, attribution disabled). It runs the existing `scrub-experiment-issue-tldrs` + `organize-experiments` skills. Recommend keeping `schedule_cron` advisory (hand-author the workflow, as today) rather than adding a metadata→workflow generator — it matches existing practice and avoids a meta-layer.

3. **Generation step → newcomer docs/teasers.** Extend the reaper to emit a short teaser per recently-updated experiment (title, author, ongoing/finished, one-paragraph TL;DR, top W&B numbers via the `itemize` script's existing `wandb.Api()` path, links) into a new `docs/reports/recent-experiments.md` (or `docs/blog/`), surfaced in `mkdocs.yml`. This is the bulk of the new code and the main design decision: dedicated blog dir vs. an auto-generated section in the existing report index.

4. **Author/status metadata.** Derive author from issue creator and ongoing/finished from issue state + a `tldr`/conclusion signal; render in the teaser page.

**Open questions for a human before implementation:**
- Blog teasers as a new `docs/blog/` surface, or an auto-generated section in `docs/reports/index.md`?
- Should generated teasers land as auto-merge PRs (like doc-drift) or be committed directly?
- Is publishing to the public `marin.community` site in scope, or only the in-repo MkDocs docs?
- Keep `schedule_cron` advisory (hand-authored workflows) or build a metadata→workflow generator?

I can take #1 (the issue template) as a first small PR once the field wording is confirmed; the rest should wait on the design answers above.
