spillover_issues.author: ravwojdyla-agent
spillover_issues.body:
## Description

Add a DaemonSet-equivalent primitive to Iris: **run exactly one instance of a workload on every node of a category, for that node's lifetime**, automatically tracking autoscaler churn. Iris can schedule discrete jobs but cannot express "one per node of scale group S" — constraints are positive-match only and coscheduling `group_by` is the opposite (gang affinity), so there is no spread/anti-affinity operator today.

Motivating consumer: smallquery's warm worker fleet (#6761), which must cover every preemptible VM. Generalizes to node-local log shippers, metric exporters, and cache/proxy sidecars.

Design + research + spec: `.agents/projects/iris_daemon/{design.md,research.md,spec.md}` (design-doc PR forthcoming).

Approach (Route A, committed v1):
- `DaemonSpec` declared in cluster YAML (sibling to `scale_groups:`), selector = a scale group + optional constraints.
- Controller-side `DaemonReconciler` maintains "one running daemon task per matching live worker" by **pinning each instance to a worker id** (HARD constraint) — sidesteps the missing spread operator — and reuses the autoscaler's worker join/leave signal. Node loss tears down for free via task↔worker binding; reconciler only ever creates.
- Discovery via EndpointService (`<endpoint_name>/<worker_id>` prefix); supervision/health/preemption accounting inherited because a daemon is a task.
- Recommended opportunistic shape: BATCH band + zero `cpu_millicores` + hard `memory_bytes`.
- Read-only `DaemonService` proto (`ListDaemons`/`GetDaemon`); `iris daemon list/status` CLI.

Out of scope v1: Route B bootstrap sidecar (`WorkerConfig.sidecar_containers`), dynamic RPC-created daemons, cross-scale-group selectors, rolling updates.

### Definition of Done

- [ ] Design-doc PR merged (`.agents/projects/iris_daemon/`); resource-accounting policy (`reserve_memory`) blessed by Iris owners
- [ ] `DaemonSpec` config + `DaemonReconciler` maintain the one-per-matching-worker invariant
- [ ] Reconciler unit tests pass across worker add/remove/restart and spec add/change/delete
- [ ] Churn integration test on an Iris dev cluster: scale up/down + kick instances, fleet re-converges, endpoints reflect live set
- [ ] `DaemonService` status RPCs + `iris daemon` CLI land
- [ ] Works on GCP/TPU and k8s/CoreWeave backends

spillover_issues.body:
## Description

["Hubs or Fringes: Pretraining Data Selection via Web Graph Centrality"](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.11499) (Badoni, Chen, Wang) proposes using web-graph centrality — PageRank, betweenness, Katz — computed over the crawl hyperlink graph as a pretraining data-selection signal. Documents from high-centrality "hub" pages are prioritized over "fringe" pages; the authors report downstream benchmark gains over random and fringe-based selection.

Open question: **should we compute a centrality feature for our documents and use it in the next data mix?**

Things to scope before committing:
- Do we retain the hyperlink graph (source/outlink structure) needed to compute centrality, or only extracted text? Centrality requires the graph, which most text-only pipelines discard.
- Cost/feasibility of building a web-scale link graph and running PageRank/Katz at our corpus scale.
- How a centrality score would compose with our existing quality classifiers — additive signal vs. redundant with what fasttext/Luxical-style filters already capture.
- A small ablation: tag a sample with centrality buckets and check correlation with existing quality scores and with downstream eval, before any full-mix integration.

### Definition of Done

- Decision recorded (adopt / reject / needs-experiment) with rationale.
- If adopt or needs-experiment: a concrete plan for (a) where the link graph comes from, (b) which centrality metric, (c) how the feature enters the data-mix selection, and (d) the ablation that would justify inclusion.

spillover_issues.author: dlwh
spillover_issues.body:
## Background
In #6070, the [PPL circuit-coverage gap dashboard](https://marin.community/analysis/ppl-circuit-coverage-gap/) showed Marin 32B lagging Qwen3 32B on short deterministic continuations: arithmetic, string/token manipulation, exact character tracking, and literal formatting. #6236 tracks adding new task families, but existing tasks also need more surface diversity so models do not overfit a single prompt shape.

## Description
Add compact template variants for existing `experiments/evals/ppl_circuit_coverage_v2.py` tasks. This is intended as a bounded contributor task: pick one existing task, add several alternate surface forms, inspect local samples, and verify target-only supervised formatting still holds.

The goal is not to add scaffolding. Keep examples Tufte-style: completed few-shot lines followed by one held-out completion prefix. Avoid labels such as `Family:`, `Task:`, `Prompt:`, `worked examples`, `held-out query`, `answer:`, or `Final answer:`.

Example target shape:

```text
text = "abcdef"; text[1:5:2] -> 'bd'
text = "marin"; text[0:4:1] -> 'mari'
text = "́kder/ejehcp"; text[6:11:1] -> 
```

with supervised `output` containing only:

```text
'ejehc'
```

Good first template-diversity targets:

- `string_slicing`: Python slice notation, prose-light `slice(text,start,stop,step)`, table-like `text | start | stop | step ->`.
- `json_field_reemit`: dot paths, bracket paths, compact `object/path -> value`.
- `csv_tsv_transforms`: delimiter names, visible separators, quoted-field variants.
- `carry_addition` / `borrow_subtraction`: vertical arithmetic, inline arithmetic, digit-array forms.
- `line_column_offsets`: `line:col`, JSON object, and compact tuple surfaces.
- `markdown_table_padding` / `outline_indentation`: vary content while preserving exact final formatting.

Suggested workflow:

1. Pick one existing task from `PPL_CIRCUIT_COVERAGE_V2_SLICES`.
2. Add a small set of surface templates inside that task's generator or a local helper.
3. Keep metadata sufficient to recompute the target independently.
4. Generate local samples:
   `uv run python -c 'from experiments.evals.ppl_circuit_coverage_v2 import write_local_sample; write_local_sample("/tmp/ppl_circuit_v2_sample", examples_per_config=36)'`
5. Inspect at least 36 examples for the task. Check ambiguity, target leakage, escaping, and accidental task telegraphing.
6. Run:
   `uv run --with pytest --with pytest-timeout pytest -m "not slow" tests/evals/test_ppl_circuit_coverage_v2.py -q`
7. Include five representative before/after examples in the PR description.

### Definition of Done
- One existing task has at least five compact surface variants, or a clear rationale for fewer variants if the task is format-constrained.
- Generated local samples show the variants are actually used.
- Supervised `input` ends before the held-out answer, and `output` contains only the final answer plus newline.
- Tests cover no target leakage and no banned scaffold strings for the changed task.
- The PR links this issue and includes five representative generated examples.

spillover_issues.author: ClassicLarry
spillover_issues.body:
## Summary

Residual-stream (hidden_dim) scaling on the fast_track MLA + Inkling MoE stack, and the full architecture path that got there from the GQA baseline. All runs are **data-matched** (`--match data`) to the baseline token budget per rung, so the quality metric is an equal-data comparison. **Result metric: `eval/paloma/macro_loss`** (lower is better).

**Final conclusion:** at these layer depths, **2× residual-stream scaling is ~neutral on FLOP compute-efficiency (0.99–1.03×) but a positive wall-clock win (1.13–1.28×) once MFU is accounted for** — the wider matmuls run at much higher utilization (MFU roughly doubles). 3× residual is a net-FLOP loss (0.84–0.92×) but still a wall-clock win (1.10–1.33×).

Branch: [`fast_track_mla_inkling`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/fast_track_mla_inkling) @ `7cffe00c3f`
Launcher: [`experiments/grug/fast_track/launch.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/fast_track_mla_inkling/experiments/grug/fast_track/launch.py)

## Initiating prompt (verbatim)

> now lets add a variation where we scale the residual stream by 2x. then another where we scale it by 3x. for all of these, have the step count match the baseline, and have the LR match the baseline. Then do another 8 where we let the LR rescale with the new hidden_dim. flops should be relatively similar, since only a small portion of the flops are hidden_dim->kv, ->q, o->hidden_dim, and hidden_dim->latent, and hidden_dim->vocab. before kicking off these 8x2, list out the flops of these vs their baselines.

## Setup

- Ladder rungs d512 / d768 / d1024 / d1280, one 8×H100 node each, `SEQ_LEN=4096`, tokenizer `hero-bpe-v16384` (vocab 16384), MoE `MOE_TPP=60` data budget.
- Data-matched steps per rung: 2413 / 7005 / 9366 / 16839 (tokens 1.27 / 3.67 / 9.82 / 17.66 B).
- "New baseline" stack = **MLA + Inkling rel-pos bias (RoPE dropped, 128-dim content-only heads) + output latent + no shared experts + top-12 routing + Q/O latent = hidden/2, KV latent = 512 + adam-routed bias weights.**
- Residual scaling = widen `hidden_dim` by N×, **all internal module dims pinned at baseline** (heads, MLA/MoE latents, intermediate); only the residual↔module boundary projections grow. Fan-in-correct init applied.

## Path from GQA → the new baseline (Paloma macro loss)

| config | d512 | d768 | d1024 | d1280 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GQA+RoPE baseline (`fasttrack-moe`) | 3.1559 | 2.8723 | 2.6330 | 2.5036 |
| GQA + Inkling bias | 3.1518 | 2.8593 | — | — |
| MLA + Inkling | 3.1384 | 2.8424 | 2.6104 | 2.4845 |
| MLA + Inkling + output-latent | 3.1448 | 2.8459 | 2.6183 | 2.4889 |
| MLA + olat + no-shared + top-12 | 3.1577 | 2.8571 | 2.6253 | 2.4985 |
| **new baseline (+ Q/O latent=hidden/2)** | 3.1589 | 2.8542 | 2.6246 | 2.4951 |

Takeaways: **MLA+Inkling beats GQA** (both RoPE and inkling baselines) and the gap widens with scale; dropping shared experts + top-12 + Q/O-latent compression is roughly loss-neutral vs plain MLA while buying inference/KV efficiency.

## Headline: residual-stream scaling (Paloma macro loss)

| config | d512 | d768 | d1024 | d1280 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| new baseline | 3.1589 | 2.8542 | 2.6246 | 2.4951 |
| residual ×2 | 3.1031 | 2.8173 | 2.5926 | 2.4699 |
| residual ×3 | 3.0851 | 2.8102 | 2.5846 | 2.4604 |
| **gain ×2** | **+0.056** | **+0.037** | **+0.032** | **+0.025** |
| **gain ×3** | **+0.074** | **+0.044** | **+0.040** | **+0.035** |

(LR-fixed vs LR-rescaled were interchangeable everywhere, ≤0.002 macro loss — shown: LR-rescaled.)

## FLOP efficiency vs MFU / wall-clock

Using the README MoE scaling law `L = 1.2 + 58.67·C^(−0.0842)` (L∞=1.2, α=0.0842): `baseline-needs` = compute multiple the baseline would need to match the residual's loss; `actual FLOPs` = the residual's per-token FLOP multiplier (= total, data-matched); `wall-clock` = data-eff × throughput ratio.

| rung / mult | loss gain | actual FLOPs | baseline-needs | **FLOP-eff** | tps ratio | **wall-clock** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| d512 ×2 | +0.056 | 1.39× | 1.41× | **1.02×** | 0.91× | **1.28×** |
| d512 ×3 | +0.074 | 1.77× | 1.58× | 0.89× | 0.84× | 1.33× |
| d768 ×2 | +0.037 | 1.32× | 1.31× | **0.99×** | 0.92× | **1.20×** |
| d768 ×3 | +0.044 | 1.64× | 1.38× | 0.84× | 0.85× | 1.16× |
| d1024 ×2 | +0.032 | 1.27× | 1.31× | **1.03×** | 0.93× | **1.21×** |
| d1024 ×3 | +0.040 | 1.54× | 1.40× | 0.91× | 0.85× | 1.19× |
| d1280 ×2 | +0.025 | 1.25× | 1.26× | **1.01×** | 0.90× | **1.13×** |
| d1280 ×3 | +0.035 | 1.50× | 1.38× | 0.92× | 0.79× | 1.10× |

- **×2 is FLOP-break-even at every scale (0.99–1.03×)** — the residual-width params trade against compute at the compute-optimal frontier rate. Structural, not coincidence.
- **×2 is a wall-clock win (1.13–1.28×)** because the wider residual lifts MFU sharply (e.g. d768 baseline 7.2 → ×2 11.9 → ×3 17.1).
- **×3 is net-FLOP-negative (0.84–0.92×)** (diminishing loss gains vs linear FLOP growth) but still wall-clock-positive.
- Why ×2 is only neutral (not positive) on FLOPs: the Q/O/MoE latent ports are `hidden/2` (proportional), so widening the residual doubles both the useful state and the port cost. Fixing those ports to smaller *absolute* dims would drop the FLOP multiplier and turn ×2 into a net-FLOP win — untested follow-up.

## Scale (d1280, per-token / total)

| config | hidden | active params | lm_head | tokens | train FLOPs (incl lm_head) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| baseline | 1280 | 313M | 21M | 17.7B | 35.3e18 |
| residual ×2 | 2560 | 377M | 42M | 17.7B | 44.4e18 |
| residual ×3 | 3840 | 442M | 63M | 17.7B | 53.5e18 |

## Supporting ablations

- **QK-norm** (non-parametric RMS on per-head q/k): keep it. Removing it costs ~0.003–0.02 macro loss at every rung; `qk_mult=1` does not recover. Canonical MLA omits QK-norm, but it helps here.
- **LatentMoE compression (latent/4, flop-neutral)**: "more experts, not fatter." Spending the saved FLOPs on 2× experts (768 total / top-16) beats fattening the intermediate at both scales, recovering ~half the compression penalty:
  - d512: baseline 3.1559 · 2×-experts 3.1787 · fat-experts 3.1992
  - d768: baseline 2.8723 · 2×-experts 2.8902 · fat-experts 2.9091
- **Expert gate/up init sweep** (latent experts have fan-in=latent, not hidden): optimum at the fan-in-correct value, but only ~0.0025–0.005 macro loss — a correctness fix, not a lever.
- **LR treatment** (residual LR-fixed vs rescaled): indistinguishable (≤0.002).

## Excluded / caveats

- `ink-gqa-latdiv4-exp2-d1280` is a **broken run** (loss rose vs its own d1024: 2.66 → 2.83) — excluded.
- GQA+Inkling only ran d512/d768. LatentMoE more-vs-fat and gate/up sweep only d512/d768.

## W&B runs (project `marin-community/marin_moe`)

Progression: `fasttrack-moe-{d512,d768,d1024,d1280}`, `ink-moe-{d512,d768}-re512d`, `ink-mla-{d512,d768,d1024,d1280}-re512-adam-f`, `ink-mla-olat512-{...}-re512-adam-f`, `ink-mla-olat-nosh-k12-{...}`, `ink-mla-nosh-k12-qoh2-{...}`
Residual: `ink-mla-nb-resid{2,3}x-{lrfix,lrscale}-{d512,d768,d1024,d1280}`
Ablations: `ink-mla-nb-noqknorm[-qkm1]-{...}`, `ink-gqa-latdiv4-exp2-{...}`, `ink-gqa-lat4-2xexp-{d512,d768b}`, `ink-gqa-lat4-gu{1p0,1p4,2p0,2p8,4p0}-{d512,d768}`

Run URL pattern: `https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/<run-name>`

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
The idea here was to make residual stream scaling extremely cheap (small vocab, latent projections on everything), then see if scaling it gave big boost to model quality for small change in flops. 2x scaling of the residual stream ends up being roughly flop neutral (maybe a slight boost if we retune its compute optimal ratio). The main gain here is on MFU. However the gains are not big enough to indicate its doing anything special. Basically, we just get gains proportional to the flops we spend.

What is looking reasonable is MLA + Inkling relative position bias + keeping QK-Norm (which is valid with MLA now, as seen in https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16310). Inkling relative position bias lets us have a clean 128 dim head.

spillover_issues.author: ClassicLarry
spillover_issues.body:
## TL;DR

Decouple the attention/MLP FLOPs from the residual-stream width so that scaling the residual
stream out is cheap, then measure how Paloma macro loss varies as a function of residual-stream
size at **fixed** attention/MoE compute.

The MoE already projects the token down to a latent (½ width) for the experts. This experiment
mirrors that on the attention path: a learnable-RMS-norm latent down-projection before attention
input and a plain up-projection on the output (no norm, mirroring the MoE up-projection). With both
attention and MLP living in the fixed-size latent space, the only params/FLOPs that grow with the
residual stream are the embedding, lm_head, the four latent down/up projections, the router, the
shared experts, and the norms. Because the vocab is small (16k), FLOPs grow slowly with residual width.

## Method

- **New baseline** = current fast_track MoE + attention latent projection (down w/ learnable RMSNorm,
  up w/o norm), at the family width (d512 → latent 256, d768 → latent 384).
- **Residual-width sweep** (d512 family): residual ∈ {384, 512, 640, 768, 1024, 1536} (base −128, base,
  +128, +256, +512, +1024), holding latent dim and every attention/MoE param size fixed at the base.
- Repeat for the **d768 family**: residual ∈ {640, 768, 896, 1024, 1280, 1792}.
- Optimizer recipe (LR/β2/ε) and token budget are pinned to the family baseline so only residual
  width varies. Data-matched, batch 128, seq 4096, on cw-us-east-02a. No checkpoints; eval on.
- 12 runs total (6 per family). Report Paloma macro loss vs residual width, with a FLOPs table.

## Exact prompt

> follow agent.md and lets try a new idea. First for the new baseline, take the moe and add a latent
> projection with learnable rms norm before the attn layer input. So similar to how MoE projects down
> to half, project attn down to half. then same on the output side, but output side doesn't need a
> learnable rms norm (mirror moe). So run that. then lets take the d512, and update the residual
> stream to -128, +128, +256, +512. keeping the latent dim size and moe/attn param sizes all the same.
> then repeat this on the d768 one. So 10 runs in total. The main idea here is we want to decouple the
> attn and mlp flops from the size of the residual stream. which makes scaling out the residual stream
> cheap. So we want to see how model quality varies as a function of residual stream size. Since vocab
> size is small, flops as a function of residual stream is small. also do +1024. Include a table with
> flops for each.

## Experiment: multi-latent MoE (per-expert latent projections)

### Initiating prompt (verbatim)

> ok now follow agent.md and lets try multi-latent moe. first to just get our bearings, take the baseline and move the latent projections into the routed experts, so each expert has their own latent projections. this means we need to pass the full activation to the target GPU. Still able a learnable rms-norm after the latent projection in, so each expert needs its own rms norm too. make sure these latent projections still route to Muon correctly.

### Idea

Baseline LatentMoE uses one **shared** `w_latent_down (d→lat)` + shared `latent_norm` + shared
`w_latent_up (lat→d)`, so all experts share a single latent subspace. This variant gives **each
expert its own** latent-down, learnable latent RMS-norm, and latent-up — each expert selects its own
subspace. The all-to-all then transports the **full d-dim** activation (≈`d/lat`× ≈2× more dispatch
bytes) instead of the compressed latent.

Motivation: our LatentMoE latent-compression runs showed a real quality penalty vs uncompressed
(recovered ~half by "more experts, not fatter"); a shared rank-`lat` bottleneck across all experts is
a prime suspect. Per-expert subspaces test whether that shared bottleneck is the cost.

### Implementation (behind `per_expert_latent`, default off → shared path byte-identical; hero-safe)

Branch: `multi-latent-moe` (off the baseline + PR#9287 budget fix). Edit points and the CPU/GPU
verification plan are in [`.agents/projects/multi-latent-moe.md`](../blob/multi-latent-moe/.agents/projects/multi-latent-moe.md):
model.py `MoEMLP`, `grug_moe.py` `MoEExpertMlp`/`moe_mlp`, `_moe/ep_fixed_pooled_wave_all_to_all.py`
`_compute_pooled` (+ CPU fallback), `optimizer.py` `create_mask`, `launch.py` flag.

Per-expert weights: `w_latent_down [E,d,lat]`, `latent_norm_gain [E,lat]`, `w_latent_up [E,lat,d]`.
Optimizer routing (explicit ask): the 3-D latent matrices → **muonh** (matrix catch-all, like
w_gate/up/down); the per-expert **norm gain** → **adam** (guarded by name so it doesn't hit the
ndim→muonh fallback).

### Result metric
`eval/paloma/macro_loss` (data-matched ladder), vs the baseline / shared-latent LatentMoE.

### Status
Design + plan + branch landed; implementation in progress behind the flag.

The checked-in SkyRL benchmark commands do not supply the inputs expected by the launcher. PR #9289 exposed three launch failures in [`snowball_eagle_speculators.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/cc1ab737d9f5f307d979405c869c6f2176a0ea54/experiments/post_training/snowball_eagle_speculators.py).

[`resolve_daytona_rl_key`](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/a39f32b296bf8a643a0c0203572e108bc4c34981/cloud/iris/iris_backend.py#L828-L856) reads `DAYTONA_RL_API_KEY`, then maps it to the worker's `DAYTONA_API_KEY`. The agentic arms in [r4](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fpower%2Fsnowball-eagle-s3-e2e-20260921-r4) exited before Iris child submission with `no Daytona RL key available`.
- `skyrl_smoke` in `lib/marin/src/marin/rl/skyrl.py` first added `trainer.callbacks` to generated YAML. The request builder emitted `trainer.callbacks=...`; Hydra rejected the missing structured-config key in [r3](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fpower%2Fsnowball-eagle-s3-e2e-20260921-r3). The branch currently embeds `++trainer.callbacks=...` in experiment-side overrides.
- `models/snowball-eagle3-speculators@2026.09.21` recorded the zero-field marker `marin.execution.artifact.Artifact`. The current graph loads the same path as the zero-field marker `marin.rl.skyrl.EagleDraftArtifact`, so the trained arms failed with `ArtifactTypeMismatchError`. Recovery required backing up and editing `.artifact.json`; the weights and payload contract were unchanged.

`skyrl_smoke` suppresses checkpoint and HF-export callbacks, but it still computes policy log probabilities and executes an optimizer step after the measured rollout. A benchmark helper should stop after reward and rollout-metric postprocessing.

Reproduce:

1. Run the TaskTrove smoke command documented in `experiments/post_training/tasktrove/rl_smoke.py` with `-e DAYTONA_API_KEY ...`; the MarinSkyRL launcher cannot resolve its coordinator credential.
2. Build `skyrl_smoke` from a base trainer mapping with no `callbacks` key and pass the resulting request to MarinSkyRL without the branch's `++` override; Hydra reports `Key 'callbacks' is not in struct`.
3. Launch the trained arm in `snowball_eagle_speculators.py` against `models/snowball-eagle3-speculators@2026.09.21`; loading the existing zero-field `Artifact` record as `EagleDraftArtifact` fails before child submission.

Expected: a checked-in Marin SkyRL benchmark command propagates its required credentials, selects benchmark callbacks through the public API, performs no policy update/checkpoint/export work, and handles compatible zero-field artifact-marker migrations through a supported path.

Done when:

- Marin declares the coordinator credentials required by each SkyRL workload. Checked-in examples either pass the canonical `DAYTONA_RL_API_KEY` or omit manual mapping; the launcher maps it to the worker-facing `DAYTONA_API_KEY`.
- `skyrl_smoke`, or its replacement benchmark helper, selects inference and logging callbacks without experiment code containing Hydra `+` or `++` syntax.
- Benchmark execution stops before policy log-probability computation and optimizer work. It still emits `vllm/spec_decode_mean_acceptance_length`, `timing/generate`, response-token totals, and `reward/avg_raw_reward`.
- A marker migration limited to zero-field `Artifact` subclasses either fails during planning with an exact supported migration command or uses a checked-in migration tool that preserves provenance and creates a backup.
- Hermetic tests cover request construction, canonical-to-worker credential mapping, and compatible marker migration. A bounded live Iris/Daytona smoke, gated on the required secret, verifies rollout telemetry and the absence of checkpoint and export artifacts.

Per-node model and checkpoint staging is tracked separately in [MarinSkyRL #713](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/issues/713).

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 The full drafting benchmark exposed another launch failure. One eight-rank vLLM DP group collided on port 26128; vLLM retried rank 0 alone on port 23834 while ranks 1–7 kept waiting on 26128. SkyRL then hid the failed generation behind `ray.wait(..., num_returns=len(refs))` until its 1,800-second startup timeout, holding the 96-H100 gang throughout.

The benchmark was cancelled. marin-community/vllm#74 makes multi-rank port collisions fail instead of changing one rank’s port, and marin-community/MarinSkyRL#716 tears down the actor gang on the first failed readiness reference.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 The credential contract is workload-dependent, not merely a naming mismatch. The canonical `DAYTONA_RL_API_KEY` reaches workers correctly, but the RL account rejects the TaskTrove Dockerfile with `400 declarative builds are not allowed`. All 128 agent rollouts in r11 hit that capability error. The same benchmark in r12, launched with the existing `DAYTONA_DATA_API_KEY` secret mapped to the worker-facing `DAYTONA_API_KEY`, has passed sandbox creation and is executing terminal-agent inference.

The fix should let a SkyRL workload declare which Daytona credential and capabilities it needs, then resolve that declaration at the coordinator boundary. A TaskTrove source containing an `environment/Dockerfile` must request a credential that permits declarative builds. It should not silently receive the restricted RL credential merely because the caller is an RL benchmark. Add a preflight or capability-specific error before the GPU job launches, and update the TaskTrove smoke example accordingly.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 r12 exposed a further benchmark-path mismatch. The step-wise trajectory runner clamps each request to the remaining model context, but the Harbor HTTP path forwards Terminus requests with `max_tokens=4096`. Once a clipped prompt reaches 28,673 tokens, vLLM rejects the 32,769-token total against Snowball's 32,768-token limit. Harbor classifies this as `ContextLengthExceededError` and the benchmark masks it to a zero reward, so it is bounded rather than a job hang, but it makes rollout completion and reward depend on an avoidable transport error.

The benchmark helper should propagate one context budget through the agent and HTTP serving boundary, account for generation-template tokens, clamp the requested completion length before vLLM validation, and end a trajectory with `stop_reason=length` when no budget remains. Add parity coverage against `trajectory_runners.step_wise.clamp_generation_tokens`.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 r12 also showed that SkyRL’s first-batch group-admission timeout is not workload-aware. The TaskTrove arm was still producing valid terminal-agent traffic when it failed exactly at the default 1,800 seconds with `GroupAdmissionStalledError`; a prompt group can include four trials, each with a 600-second agent timeout and bounded retries. The experiment now sets 3,600 seconds explicitly, but the benchmark API should derive or require a bound consistent with the trajectory timeout and retry envelope, and its progress detector should distinguish active production from a true admission stall.

Credential inspection has a separate redaction gap: Iris presents environment values redacted in submitted argv, but a raw job-config query can return the environment mapping unredacted. The query/API serialization path should apply the same secret-field redaction policy before returning job configuration. No credential values are included here.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body: 🤖 The stuck benchmark exposed a second launch-contract bug: `skyrl_smoke` disabled export callbacks but still ran the full trainer, so rollout-only measurements entered group admission, constructed policy workers, ran the optimizer, and could stall replacing unusable groups. PR #9289 now routes smoke runs through the dedicated `generate` entrypoint with validation data and an 8-node inference-only topology. MarinSkyRL PR #717 disables Ray-local retries for this entrypoint, uses the shared job supervisor, performs explicit teardown, and publishes final cumulative inference/speculation counters. r14 is exercising the corrected path on the same three agentic arms.

spillover_issues.author: lukedhlee
spillover_issues.body:
I evaluated the Snowball R2E-Gym RL checkpoints under [Eval Policy v0.1](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9193) (harbor `7b18505a`, the recovery job files from `8aa9a354`, one trial per task, 16 concurrent, 32,768 / 8,192 tokens, terminus-2 defaults, Daytona). Two things came out that I think matter beyond Snowball. Full write-up with the training-side story: https://gist.github.com/lukedhlee/01897efa3ae7c474732c61d35150a43a (Part III).

**Checkpoints.** Base = [laion/snowball-67b-a2b-sft-s3-nemotron-terminal-step1888](https://huggingface.co/laion/snowball-67b-a2b-sft-s3-nemotron-terminal-step1888). RL = GRPO on R2E-Gym repository-fix tasks with terminus-2 (terminal only), [old stack update 36](https://huggingface.co/laion/snowball-67b-a2b-rl-r2egym-oldstack-step36) and [new stack update 24](https://huggingface.co/laion/snowball-67b-a2b-rl-r2egym-newstack-step24), the pick. Two later checkpoints are in the figure too: [update 48](https://huggingface.co/laion/snowball-67b-a2b-rl-r2egym-newstack-step48) of the same run, and update 24 continued for 24 more updates on a refreshed pool of 1,247 tasks. Training ran terminus-2 with summarization **off** at 49,152 input / 16,384 output tokens.

### 1. The RL gain is in-distribution: SWE-bench Verified moves, Terminal-Bench 2 does not

![Under Marin's eval policy, the RL gain shows on SWE-bench and not on Terminal-Bench 2](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/lukedhlee/f50158cdcffb2a6367d26f63432a3f2a/raw/3998f0fb24fe70f1d6aa7d55fa575b2255bc51e9/fig5_policy_id_vs_ood.png)

Whiskers are 95% intervals, about ±8 points with one trial per task. Paired on SWE-bench the new checkpoint solves 15 tasks the base does not and loses 4 (12 to 8 against the old stack). On TB2 the base and the two RL picks are within noise and update 24 is lowest in every setting I tried. Training longer does not move SWE-bench: update 48 scores 25 against update 24's 23 and wins 13 tasks while losing 11, the same churn two identical runs of update 24 show (23 and 24, disagreeing on 22 tasks). The refreshed pool did not buy transfer: 17 on SWE-bench, losing 16 tasks to update 24 and winning 10, and 5 of 89 on TB2. The one hint of anything is update 48 on TB2, 9 of 87 against 4, winning 6 and losing 1, still inside a one-trial interval. TB2 denominators are scored tasks; 0 to 4 trials per run were lost to infrastructure (mostly the agent running `pkill -f` inside the sandbox, which kills harbor's own tmux command), inside the 10 % allowance, and counting them as failures does not change the order.

R2E-Gym and SWE-bench are the same kind of work, a Python repo with failing tests to fix, and that is where the 11 points show up. The RL checkpoint declares done fast (median 4 minutes of agent time per SWE-bench task vs 21 for the base), which is what finishing inside the window looks like on repo fixes and what giving up early looks like on TB2's long build-and-verify tasks.

### 2. Summarization helps the RL checkpoint, even though it was never trained with it

SWE-bench random-100 at the policy setting, at 32k with summarization off, and at the training setting (49k/16k, off), for base and the new checkpoint:

![How each SWE-bench trial ended, by terminus-2 setting](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/lukedhlee/f50158cdcffb2a6367d26f63432a3f2a/raw/cac4e15e3f7d8f684aa35b7bddb24ec58bdd5042/fig6_summarization_context.png)

All 600 trials scored, no infrastructure losses. A trial that runs out of context stops and is graded as it stands. Caveat: the base's two summarization-off rows were served at temperature 0.7 with a repetition penalty of 1.1 by mistake; every other row is temperature 1.0 with no penalty. It cannot change the picture for a model that overflows on 97 of 100 tasks, but those two rows are not sampler-paired with the rest. Agent requests in all runs set `skip_special_tokens: false` so the think markers stay in the transcript; Marin's agentic launcher does not set this flag today. A paired probe says it does not matter for the score: the RL checkpoint at the policy setting scores 23 and 24 of 100 with the flag (two runs) and 23 without it, and the two flag-on runs disagree on as many tasks (22) as flag-on vs flag-off (23), so per-task differences are sampling noise at temperature 1.0.

- The base cannot work without summarization: 94 to 97 of 100 trials overflow at either budget. RL cut that to 42 at the training budget.
- The RL checkpoint's best number is with summarization on, which training never used, and its lead over base is the same size in every setting (+11, +5, +11). RL improved the task skill rather than fitting one context regime.
- Summarization at 32k beats a 49k window without it, for both models. 23 vs 19 is inside the one-trial noise; a 3-trial rerun (~15 GH200 node-hours) would settle it.

**Takeaways for the policy.** Keeping terminus-2's summarization on in v0.1 is the right call for this model family, and it is not a mismatch with how the checkpoint was trained. SWE-bench random-100 is the ID leg that detects R2E-Gym RL; TB2 does not, at this checkpoint.

**Reproduction.** Stack, task revisions (DCAgent2/terminal_bench_2, DCAgent2/swebench-verified-random-100-folders `0c553bd6`) and the variant configs are in the gist's "Policy evaluation" section. Job directories and traces are on JSC Jupiter; happy to attach any trial.

comments.author: lukedhlee
comments.body:
Follow-up: I put SFT in front of the same RL and it did not beat RL from the base. Same Eval Policy v0.1 setting as above (harbor `7b18505a`, one trial per task, 16 concurrent, 32,768 / 8,192 tokens, terminus-2, summarization on, Daytona). Training-side story and the SFT diagnosis: https://gist.github.com/lukedhlee/48185da748a200d44f7fe31431054e37.

**What ran.** Two SFTs of the base on Kimi K2 SWE-smith traces (standard, and "TailSFT" = the same recipe with the filtered objective of [arXiv 2608.25756](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.25756): each step drops the 25 % of documents whose loss has fallen the most against their loss under the initial model, so training concentrates on what is not fit yet), each followed by 24 GRPO updates on its own learnable R2E-Gym band (the training tasks it solved 1–7 times out of 8 in a screen of the same 1,247-task pool; 454 and 453 tasks, the same count as the base's band). Same recipe as the base + RL row: lr 5e-7, staleness 2, no KL, 12 nodes per arm.

![SFT then RL, SWE-bench and TB2 under Eval Policy v0.1](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/lukedhlee/f50158cdcffb2a6367d26f63432a3f2a/raw/658683eb60aa0fc94be408b54a038f280a8c1642/fig6_sft_to_rl.png)

| checkpoint | SWE-bench Verified random-100 | Terminal-Bench 2 |
|---|---|---|
| base (SFT) | 12 / 100 | 6 / 84 |
| Kimi SWE-smith SFT | 7 / 100 | 3 / 89 |
| TailSFT | 11 / 99 | 2 / 89 |
| Kimi SWE-smith SFT + RL 24 | 20 / 100 | 5 / 89 |
| TailSFT + RL 24 | 13 / 100 | 6 / 88 |
| base + RL 24 (new stack, from above) | **23 / 100** | 4 / 87 |

### 1. RL repaired the standard SFT's regression, but only back to where RL from the base already was

The standard SFT lost 5 points to the base (7 vs 12, paired 4 wins / 9 losses). 24 RL updates took it to 20: it now solves 18 tasks the SFT could not and loses 5, and paired against the base it wins 14 / loses 6. Against base + RL 24 it is 8 / 11 with 12 shared, so inside one-trial noise of the 23 and not above it. On TB2 every row is within noise of the base's 6.

### 2. TailSFT started higher single-shot and RL barely moved it

TailSFT read level with the base before RL (11 vs 12) and had the steeper pass@k curve (25 vs 22 at pass@8 on this split). After the same 24 updates it is at 13: 5 unlocked, 3 lost against its own start, and 4 / 14 against base + RL 24. Both arms roughly doubled their training reward over the 24 updates and both learned to declare done more often (standard 32 % → 63 % of attempts, TailSFT 54 % → 80 %). The difference is what happened underneath: the standard SFT arm's pass@8 on its training batches rose from .69 to .84, while the TailSFT arm's stayed flat at about .74 and its reward came from finishing more often at a modestly higher reward-given-done (.30 → .58). The arm whose per-task ability actually rose is the one that moved on SWE-bench.

**Takeaway.** On this model, SFT on SWE-smith traces before R2E-Gym RL does not add to what RL from the base reaches in the same 24 updates. The traces teach a finishing style; RL rebuilt the standard SFT's task ability but only to the base + RL level, and on TailSFT it mostly rewarded the finishing style, and neither path ends above 23 / 100. These are one-trial reads, so the 20 vs 23 is a tie; the 13 is a real gap against base + RL (4 / 14 paired).

**Caveat added after a code and weight audit of the two SFT checkpoints (same day).** The TailSFT and standard checkpoints are near-replicates: they sit 5.9e-5 relative L2 apart, against a 3.4e-5 floor between two runs of the unmodified trainer and a 2.7e-4 shift for the SFT itself, and no seed was pinned. So the 13 vs 20 above is not established as a TailSFT effect; the honest reading is that two RL runs from near-identical starts diverged by 7 points on this split after 24 updates, which is the run-to-run spread of the pipeline at one trial, and the same spread applies to the 20 vs 23 comparison with base + RL. The data-side audit found the more likely cause of the SFT regression itself: 39 % of the Kimi training traces are failed trials that still end by declaring the task complete, and the traces are ten times shorter than the base's own working style, so the SFT learned when to stop, not when the fix is right.

**Reproduction.** SFT checkpoints `snowball-kimi_swesmith-sft/full-lr5e-5-ep3` and `full-lr5e-5-ep3-tail25` (export step 96), RL configs `snowball_ttband_{vansft_l454,tailsft_l453}_12n_a` with the band trees named in the gist; policy job directories on JSC Jupiter, happy to attach any trial.

comments.body:
Follow-up 2 (updated 2026-09-21 with three trials per checkpoint and two more arms): SFT on the OpenThoughts-Agent traces (IssueTasks removed) plus if-v2, with or without RST rollouts, reaches the RL-from-base level on SWE-bench without any RL. Terminal-Bench 2 does not move. RST alone collapses both.

Same Eval Policy v0.1 setting as above (harbor `7b18505a`, Daytona, terminus-2 with summarization on, 32,768 / 8,192 tokens, temperature 1.0), with two differences: 32 concurrent trials instead of 16, and three trials per checkpoint. The base was re-run three times under this setting so the rows are comparable.

**What ran.** Four SFTs of the same Stage-3 base with Levanter on 16 GH200 nodes, lr 1e-4, one epoch of a two-epoch cosine, 64 sequences of 32,768 tokens per step, 8 to 23 node-hours per arm. Data:

- OTA2 = OpenThoughts-Agent-SFT-100K without its IssueTasks slice, i.e. the SWE-smith, SuperUser and Tezos slices, 64,022 traces. IssueTasks is built from SWE-bench test issues and 255 of the 500 Verified issues appear rewritten inside it, so it is out of every reportable model.
- if-v2: 12,484 Nemotron-Gym instruction-following terminal traces (`open-athena/nemotron-gym-if-v2-qwen3.5-122b-32k-traces`). In every arm, because an OTA-only SFT loses 0.15 on held-out if-v2 tasks and this slice repairs it.
- RST: `open-athena/recursive-task-synthesis-glm-5.3-rollouts`, one rollout per task with at least 5 turns, 14,410 tasks (3,012 successes, the rest failures, kept as the OpenThoughts-Agent paper recommends). "RST successes" keeps 9,396 rollouts over the 3,014 tasks with at least one success. Zero shared word 8-grams with TB2 or Verified.

| checkpoint | SWE-bench Verified random-100 (3 trials) | pooled | Terminal-Bench 2 (3 trials) | pooled |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| base, this setting | 13 / 100, 17 / 98, 13 / 99 | 0.145 | 5 / 85, 8 / 85, 11 / 86 | 0.094 |
| A: OTA2 + if-v2, 495 steps | 23 / 99, 19 / 100, 24 / 99 | 0.221 | 5 / 88, 1 / 87, 7 / 81 | 0.051 |
| C: OTA2 + RST + if-v2, 626 steps | 27 / 100, 18 / 100, 19 / 100 | 0.213 | 3 / 87, 4 / 87, 2 / 80 | 0.035 |
| D: OTA2 + RST successes + if-v2, 517 steps | 27 / 100, 22 / 99, 23 / 100 | 0.241 | 4 / 87, 5 / 89, 7 / 88 | 0.061 |
| B: RST + if-v2, 159 steps | 3 / 100, 2 / 100, 4 / 100 | 0.030 | 0 / 86, 0 / 89, 1 / 89 | 0.004 |

Denominators are scored trials (the rest are infrastructure losses, recovered where a rerun was possible; the third TB2 trials of A and C lost their last 8 tasks when the serve node hit its wall).

![SFT arms under Eval Policy v0.1: SWE-bench, Terminal-Bench 2, and the two held-out probes](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/lukedhlee/f50158cdcffb2a6367d26f63432a3f2a/raw/41585b63e47d08fd154b5b67097fa91a7e831ca3/fig8_ota3_sft_arms.png)

### 1. Every OTA2 arm lifts SWE-bench by 7 to 10 points, the size of the RL lift, and D is the best of them by a margin inside the noise

Pooled over three trials, D reaches 72 of 299 (0.24) against the base's 43 of 297 (0.15); A and C sit at 0.22 and 0.21. The worst SFT trial (18 / 100) beats the best base trial (17 / 98), and the best SFT trials match update 24's 23 / 100 above. The mechanism is the one RL showed: agent timeouts on SWE-bench drop from 50 to 53 per 100 for the base to 28 to 37 for D (33 to 57 across the other arms). The model learned to finish repo fixes inside the window.

D beat or tied A in every trial on both benchmarks, but the pooled gap is 2 points on SWE and 1 on TB2 with a standard error near 3.5 points, and D also saw about 15 percent more tokens in its one epoch. So "RST successes help a little" is the direction, not a result yet. Adding all RST rollouts (C) buys nothing over A.

### 2. Terminal-Bench 2 does not move for any arm, and the held-out terminal probes say why

TB2 sits at 0.03 to 0.06 for the OTA2 arms against the base's 0.09, with the timeout count unchanged at 54 to 67 of 89. Two cheaper probes under the same serving load (32 + 32 concurrent agents, base re-run under the same load) give the direction:

- On 477 held-out if-v2 tasks the final checkpoints are above base, paired +0.05 (C), +0.07 (A, D), so the instruction-following slice did its job.
- On 337 held-out RST tasks, task families never seen in training, every checkpoint is below base, paired -0.03 to -0.05, and the agent-timeout count rises from 62 to between 91 and 133 of 337. The SFT makes the model slower on unfamiliar terminal tasks, which is what TB2 measures.

### 3. RST alone is not a terminal-skill dataset at this dose, it is a quitting dataset

Arm B (RST + if-v2, no OTA2) falls to 0.03 on SWE-bench and 0.004 on TB2, and its held-out RST probe drops to 0.01 from the base's 0.06. The traces explain it: 86 percent of the RST rollouts end with the agent declaring `task_complete: true` at a median of 7 turns, and 75 percent of them are failures. B learned to stop early: it finishes 315 of 333 held-out trials in a median of 16 turns and passes 1 percent. The teacher (GLM-5.3) itself passes 0.09 of the RST tasks at one attempt under this harness. The RST paper trained only on verified successes, self-rolled, at lr 3e-6, so their recipe and ours share little beyond the task generator. Dropping the failures (D) removes the harm but does not add terminal skill.

**Next.** D resumed into its second epoch, and A's one-third checkpoint on the targets, to separate dose from data; then R2E-Gym RL from D's one-third and final checkpoints, which now start 10 points above where RL from the base started.

**Reproduction.** Corpora, the RST converter and the filters are in `data/rst/` and `data/r2egym/jsc/ota3_arm.sh` on the OpenThoughts-Agent `lukedhlee/vista-moe-grpo-30b` branch; the marin stages `ota3_if`, `rst_if`, `ota3_if_rst` and `ota3_if_rstsucc` are on `lukedhlee/vista-snowball-sft`; job directories and traces on JSC Jupiter, happy to attach any trial.

spillover_issues.author: ClassicLarry
spillover_issues.body:
## Summary

Test **omni-neurons**: a dense-model variant where each layer's **MLP** reads the
concatenation of *every prior sublayer snapshot* instead of just the current
residual stream. Attention is unchanged (it still reads the residual stream).

For layer `n` the MLP input is the concatenation of:
`[embed, {attn_out_i, resid_post_attn_i, mlp_out_i, resid_post_mlp_i for each prior layer i}, attn_out_n, resid_post_attn_n]`
— each `d`-wide, so the MLP input width grows with depth as `d·(4n+3)`. The MLP
still writes a `d`-wide residual delta (asymmetric in/out).

**Research goal:** after training, inspect *where the MLP input neurons point* —
do they attend to the individual layer branch outputs (`attn_out` / `mlp_out`) or
to the accumulated residual-stream sums (`resid_post_attn` / `resid_post_mlp`)?
This is why final checkpoints are saved.

## Exact prompts

> follow agent.md and test an idea called omni-neurons. Lets use the dense model as the baseline. but save the output of every layer, and the sum after its added to the residual stream. The input to layer n will then be a concatenated list of [embed, layer0_attn_out, layer0_resid_post_attn, layer0_mlp_out, layer0_resid_post_mlp, layer1_attn_out, layer1_resid_post_attn...]. So the input dim to layer I scales with the layer. EG layer 6 will have roughly 24x wider dims. First, will this fit at d512?

> oh, lets only use omni input for mlp, not attn.

> yes, run both sizes and raise a github issue. The idea here is we want to investigate after it trains where the input neurons are pointing. To see if they are looking at the layer outputs, or the residual stream sums. So we also need to turn on final checkpoint saving.

## Feasibility (MLP-only omni, d512 dense: d=512, L=6, I=1536, seq=4096, batch=128, 8×H100)

| Item | dense baseline | omni-MLP |
|---|---|---|
| Non-embed params | 18.1M | 131.3M (7.3×) |
| Total params | 34.9M | 148.1M |
| Weights + optimizer state (14 B/param, FSDP /8) | 0.06 GB/gpu | 0.26 GB/gpu |
| Retained snapshot activations (4/layer, bf16, /8) | — | 1.68 GB/gpu |
| **Total-model FLOPs/step** (incl. attn core + embed) | 1× | **~2.9×** |

Fits trivially (single-digit GB/gpu). The binding cost is compute: ~2.9× total
FLOPs → expect ~3× slower wall-clock, so the run must show a real loss gain to
net positive on effective speedup. Params grow ≈ `L²` with depth, so the full
ladder (d1024/d1280) would get much more expensive — a gate-2 consideration.

## Implementation

Branch `fast_track_omni_mlp` @ `95a2cf0a0e` (off the baseline-budget branch).

- `model.py`: `GrugModelConfig.omni_mlp` (dense-only, default off → shared path
  byte-identical). `DenseMLP.init` gains `out_dim` (wide input, `d`-wide output).
  Heterogeneous per-layer MLP widths can't be scanned, so omni blocks are held
  **unrolled** (`Transformer.omni_blocks`) with a Python-loop forward that
  accumulates the snapshot list, per-snapshot RMSNorm (shared width-`d` gain, keeps
  snapshots magnitude-comparable), concatenates, then the wide GatedNorm + MLP.
  Each layer remat'd (`eqx.filter_checkpoint`).
- `optimizer.py`: no change needed — omni's leaves route correctly
  (`w_gate/w_up/w_down` → muonh, `rms_mlp.weight` → adam, `mlp_gated_norm` → muonh).
- `launch.py`: `--omni-mlp` flag (implies `--dense`).

Verified on CPU: per-layer widths = `d·(4i+3)` in / `d` out, non-omni path intact,
optimizer routing correct, concat bookkeeping matches. GPU forward validated by the
launched runs stepping.
